The corrected trap list\n\n1. **⚑ Ed25519 verification (Column B only).** The corpus's blueprint says \"use `verify_strict()`\"; its crypto brief says `verify_strict()` is *not* ZIP-215. Both cannot be right. **Normative answer: pin ZIP-215** — the cofactored equation `[8][S]B = [8]R + [8][k]A`, non-canonical encodings permitted, small-order points not rejected, `S < l` required — because it is the only rule under which batch and single verification agree. `ed25519-dalek` 3.0.0 (2026-07-06) *does* document ZIP-215 rules on `VerifyingKey::from_bytes` point decoding; that is decoding, not the verification equation. Use `ed25519-zebra` 4.x in Rust and `@noble/curves` with `zip215: true` in TS, and copy the four ZIP-215 bullets into your spec verbatim.\n2. **Non-canonical encoding on a hashed path.** Hash-map iteration order, protobuf field ambiguity, JSON key order. One canonical encoder, `BTreeMap` only, sort the write set before hashing, and property-test `encode(decode(b)) == b` for a million iterations before you write consensus code.\n3. **No domain separation.** A precommit signature that is also a valid transaction signature. Every hash preimage gets a one-byte tag plus `chain_id`. Freeze the full tag list on day one — changing one later is a hard fork.\n4. **Fusing `stage` and `commit`.** A rejected proposal poisons the DB unrecoverably.\n5. **Merkle odd-node duplication + caching the hash as invalid.** CVE-2012-2459, in full.\n6. **Little-endian numeric keys.** Range scans break at block 256.\n7. **Signing before fsync.** The `(height, round, step)` high-water mark lives *inside* the signer, is fsync'd before the signature is released, holds an exclusive lock, and its path is documented as \"must never be restored from backup.\"\n8. **⚑ Kubernetes double-signing.** The 2019 failure mode (restoring `priv_validator_state.json`) is well known; the 2026 one is a `Deployment` instead of a single-replica `StatefulSet`, a rolling update that briefly overlaps pods, or an HPA. All three produce two signers with one key and a tombstone. Publish the correct shape and name the anti-patterns.\n9. **Sync DB calls on the async runtime.** Every redb/RocksDB call needs `spawn_blocking`. This is the #1 cause of 2-second p95 RPC latency.\n10. **Unbounded channels.** A slow consumer becomes an OOM instead of a load-shed signal.\n11. **Trusting `CheckTx`.** It is a weak filter. A Byzantine proposer can put anything in a block. Re-validate everything inside `execute()`.\n12. **Unmetered block-boundary hooks.** Every hook is O(1) or O(k) with a hard-coded k, and can never return an error or panic.\n13. **Decoder bombs.** Cap recursion depth and check `MAX_LEN` *before* allocation. Cosmos ASA-2024-0012/0013 (Dec 2024) were exactly this: a deeply nested packet causing stack overflow and a network halt, and nested `UnpackAny` causing exponential CPU/memory that bypassed `max_tx_bytes`.\n14. **⚑ Snapshot format drift across a fork.** A pre-upgrade snapshot that no longer restores post-upgrade silently breaks all new-node onboarding, at every fork. Version the format, gate restore on the version, alert on snapshot age and `trust_hash` staleness.\n15. **⚑ Fork-boundary mempool semantics.** Revalidate everything at activation and drop failures with a distinguishable error. And expand the upgrade rehearsal beyond validators: the explorer, the indexer, the public RPC, the snapshot servers and wallet fee estimation each get their own go/no-go.\n16. **Cold start.** No user can transact without your gas token, and it exists only on your chain. Pick and build one mechanism before genesis — protocol-level fee sponsorship for the first N transactions per address, or a gated claim funded from the community pool — and write the claim → DEX pool → first CEX sequence with owners and dates.\n17. **Do not write a bridge.** Ronin $624M, Poly Network $611M, BNB Bridge $586M, Wormhole $326M, Bybit $1.436B. Wormhole ran a 19-member Guardian set with 13-of-19 supermajority and cited 29 third-party audits — that is the resourcing level of the systems that *got hacked*.\n\n---\n\n## 12. Observability: two dashboards, not one\n\n**Node health (six alerts).** `time() - last_block_timestamp > 3 × block_interval`; peers < 3 for 5 m; consensus round > 0 for 2 m; a validator missing from the last 50 blocks; disk < 20%; RPC p99 > 2 s for 10 m. ⚑ Add a seventh: `apply_block_duration_seconds / block_interval > 0.35` for 5 m — the metric that tells you the gas limit is now wrong, before rounds start cascading.\n\n**⚑ Economics and decentralisation (the dashboard the corpus omits entirely).** Page on any single operator crossing 1/3 voting power (a unilateral halt capability) and on top-3 crossing 2/3 (unilateral finality). Chart delegation drift, per-validator missed-proposal patterns, realised inflation versus the published emission curve, and the kill-criteria metrics — active addresses, non-validator transactions, TVL — so the T+26 review reads a number rather than a vibe.",

        "markdown": "> **Budget honesty first.** This is 12 weeks at **8–12 focused hours/week = 96–144 hours total**. That buys you the ability to *read* any chain's source and *design* one. It does not buy you a mainnet. The corpus's own M0–M10 build ladder is 11–19 person-weeks, and everything through launch (testing pyramid, RPC/explorer/indexer, tokenomics, genesis, ops) sums to **35–55 person-weeks ≈ 1,400–2,200 hours ≈ 3–4 years of evenings**. This curriculum is the substitute for M0–M6, not a prerequisite to it. If you finish week 12 and start building, you are at hour ~150 of ~1,600.\n\n---\n\n## Week 0 — the trunk decision (3 hours, mandatory, before week 1)\n\nThe corpus contains **four mutually exclusive top-level architectures**, each presented as *the* answer inside its own dimension. If you don't pick one now, you build an incoherent hybrid and discover the contradiction around month five. Pick an archetype; the \"out of scope\" column tells you what to stop reading.\n\n| Archetype | Trunk | Read all of | Out of scope for you |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **A — BFT appchain** (default) | Cosmos SDK v0.54.4 + CometBFT v0.39.4, own validator set, Go | ledger-model, consensus-pos-bft, frameworks-l1, testing-ops, node-apis | AuxPoW, ASERT, reorg handling, 100-block reorg caps |\n| **B — L2 / token on an existing chain** | OP Stack, or just an ERC-20 | l2-tokens-alternatives, execution-vm, node-apis | consensus (all of it), p2p, genesis ceremony, validator ops |\n| **C — from-scratch PoW coin** | SHA-256d + AuxPoW, T=120s, `MAX_REORG_DEPTH=100` | consensus-pow, ledger-model (UTXO), p2p-networking | BFT, slashing, ABCI, single-slot finality |\n| **D — from-scratch account chain** (learning) | Rust crate tree, embedded revm, sans-I/O consensus | from-scratch-blueprint, execution-vm, crypto-primitives | — this is the curriculum's default build target |\n\n**The five questions that select the archetype:** (1) Do you need Solidity and MetaMask on day one? (2) Is consensus or execution your actual differentiator, or is it an app? (3) Can you fund 15–30 professional validators for 18 months in fiat? (4) Do you need probabilistic settlement compatible with Bitcoin mining, or deterministic finality? (5) Will you ever want an EVM — including \"maybe, in v3\"?\n\n### The identity stack: exactly two viable columns\n\nThis is decided once, at genesis, and cascades into wallet reachability, hardware-wallet cost, exchange deposit derivation, explorer and indexer. The corpus decides it three times with incompatible answers. There is **no third column**.\n\n| Consequence | Column 1: EVM-compatible | Column 2: Cosmos/sovereign |\n|---|---|---|\n| Signature | secp256k1 ECDSA (EIP-155, EIP-2 low-s) | Ed25519, **ZIP-215 pinned** |\n| Address | 20-byte hex `0x…` | Bech32m (BIP-350), own HRP, 32-byte hash |\n| SLIP-44 coin type | reuse **60** — do not register | reuse **118** (Keplr recommends it for Ledger) |\n| HD derivation | BIP-32, **watch-only xpub works** | SLIP-0010 hardened-only, **no watch-only xpub** |\n| Wallet day 1 | MetaMask, free | Keplr-class, or you write an SDK |\n| Hardware wallet | Ledger's Ethereum app, free | **Rust device app, 3rd-party audit (Kudelski/Quarkslab), 6–12 months + real money** |\n| Exchange deposits | xpub derivation works | exchanges may refuse you |\n| Decimals | **18 / u256, no exceptions** | 6 / u64 — **but only if \"no EVM, ever\" is written into the frozen list** |\n\n**The decimals trap the corpus never joins up:** an 18-decimal EVM over a 6-decimal bank denom needs a conversion layer at every boundary, with truncation and dust asymmetries — a repeatedly-exploited bug class on Cosmos EVM chains. If EVM is possible *ever*, take 18 decimals and 256-bit amounts at genesis.\n\n### Frozen-at-genesis list (write it in week 1, never edit it)\n\nAddress format · hash function and every domain-separation tag · decimals and integer width · chain ID · SLIP-44 coin type · EVM-or-never · signature scheme and its accept-set (ZIP-215 vs RFC 8032-strict) · canonical codec.\n\n---\n\n## Ranking the 21 reader-supplied tutorials\n\nThey are not 21 resources. They are roughly **four ideas** — hash-linked list, leading-zero PoW, longest-chain rule, ECDSA-signed transfers — re-implemented in fourteen languages. Reading them in parallel teaches syntax, not protocol.\n\n### DO these (type every line) — 3 of 21\n\n| Tutorial | Why it earns the hours | What it omits (you must supply) |\n|---|---|---|\n| **jeiwan.net, Go, 7 parts** | The only entry with UTXO + BoltDB persistence + base58check addresses + Merkle + a Bitcoin-shaped wire protocol (`version`/`getblocks`/`inv`/`getdata`/`block`/`tx`) | Author's own TODO: *\"Instead of trusting unconditionally, we should validate every incoming block\"* (blocks, **not** txs — it does verify mempool txs). *\"We'll use ports as node identifiers.\"* Peer discovery: *\"I started implementing it, but haven't finished!\"* Single hardcoded central node. Uses `elliptic.P256()`, **not secp256k1** |\n| **lhartikk naivecoin, TS, ch. 1–5** | The only entry that ranks chains by **work** (`Σ 2^difficulty`) rather than length. Verified: `BLOCK_GENERATION_INTERVAL = 10`, `DIFFICULTY_ADJUSTMENT_INTERVAL = 10`, `isValidTimestamp` = ±60s window | No peer discovery, no persistence, no Merkle tree, no fees, O(n) whole-chain sync. `Σ 2^difficulty` is a **proxy** — it equals real work only when the target sits on a bit boundary |\n| **yukimotopress, Ruby, 6 ch.** | ~50 lines total, best on-ramp in the set. One evening, then discard | No transactions, wallets, Merkle or P2P — and it says so |\n\n### SKIM these (2–4 hours each, for one specific idea) — 6 of 21\n\n| Tutorial | Take exactly this | Ignore |\n|---|---|---|\n| conradoqg/naivecoin | The API/operator split and Swagger surface | Its own README: *\"Naivechain uses websocket for p2p… it was dropped to simplify… relying only on REST\"* — polling is not gossip |\n| nambrot/blockchain-in-js | Steps 4–7: a `UTXOPool` cached **per block** — the correct \"block = state transition\" model | Merkle and SegWit are explicitly deferred |\n| SavjeeCoin | Watch the videos for intuition | *\"⚠️ For education purposes only… by no means secure!\"* Balances by full-chain scan |\n| adilmoujahid.com | The wallet-app/node-app topology | **RSA 1024-bit PKCS#1 v1.5**, public keys used directly as addresses, no Merkle, no UTXO |\n| ecomunsing.com | 90 minutes for the state-function framing: `isValidTxn` = sum of deltas is 0, no overdraft | No PoW, no signatures, no network |\n| freeCodeCamp Scala/Akka | Actor-per-concern node structure | **Akka went BSL in Sept 2022 — use Apache Pekko** |\n\n### SKIP these — 12 of 21, with the reason\n\n| Tutorial | Why skip |\n|---|---|\n| **dvf / van Flymen (Python)** | The famous flaw, stated correctly: `valid_proof(last_proof, proof, last_hash)` *does* commit to the previous block. The defect is that **nothing about the block being mined enters the hash** — `/mine` solves against the *previous* block, then sweeps in whatever sits in `current_transactions`. A miner solves once and picks the transaction set for free. (Its `json.dumps(sort_keys=True)` is fine; the generic \"JSON key order\" warning doesn't apply here.) |\n| mycoralhealth (Go) | Strict subset of jeiwan parts 1–2; no UTXO, no persistence, no addresses |\n| Smashing Magazine | Blog-length restatement of the hash-chain; zero code you keep |\n| Crystal / Kotlin / ATS ports | Language demos. The protocol content is identical to yukimotopress at 3× the reading cost |\n| \"Tiniest Blockchain\" (Python) | ~30 lines, no PoW, no txs, no signatures. Superseded by yukimotopress in the same evening |\n| digital-alchemy | No persistence, no network, no fork choice |\n| HackerNoon entry #1 and #2 | Both superseded by **rust-state-machine** (42 steps, 7 sections, FRAME-shaped, written from scratch without the libraries) |\n| Java NoobChain | Only if Java is your sole language. No persistence, no network |\n| NaivecoinStake (beyond ch. 2) | Author concedes it *\"cannot be used in production\"*; nothing-at-stake and long-range attacks go unaddressed. Naive chain-based PoS teaches a model you must then unlearn |\n\n**The altitude none of the 21 operate at** is the comment Bitcoin Core's own developers left in `src/consensus/merkle.cpp`: *\"If you're reading this because you're learning about crypto and/or designing a new system that will use merkle trees, keep in mind that the following merkle tree algorithm has a serious flaw…\"*\n\n---\n\n## Primary sources\n\nLegend: ✓ = URL fetched and verified inside the research corpus · ○ = canonical path; contents verified, URL string reconstructed.\n\n| Source | URL | State (2026-08) | Read |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Bitcoin whitepaper | bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf ○ | canonical | Twice, week 1 |\n| **Ethereum execution-specs (EELS)** | steel.ethereum.foundation/docs/execution-specs/ ✓ | **the live spec**; maintained by the STEEL Team; branches `mainnet` + `forks/amsterdam`; CLI `ethereum-spec-evm` = t8n + b11r + state-test runner | `forks/*/fork.py`, then `vm/` |\n| Ethereum Yellow Paper | ○ | **Superseded.** README: reflects spec *\"up to the Shanghai network upgrade… block 17_034_870 (April 2023)\"*, *\"does not yet contain changes introduced by Cancun\"* | §4, §6, §9, App. H — **notation only** |\n| ethereum/execution-apis | ethereum.github.io/execution-apis/ ✓ | live | Week 11 |\n| **ethereum/execution-spec-tests** | ○ | **archived** — *\"All code from this repository has been migrated to ethereum/execution-specs\"*; `eest.ethereum.org` redirects to the steel docs | Fixture formats, week 10 |\n| Bitcoin Core | bitcoincore.org ✓ | **v31.1 (2026-07-08)**, v31.0 (2026-04-20) | Weeks 3, 5, 7, 11 |\n| Mastering Bitcoin 3e | ○ | Antonopoulos + Harding, Dec 2023, CC BY-SA 4.0. A | v0.38.26 (2026-08-13) is the *newest tag* and README says *\"Currently supported versions include: v0.38.x\"*; **v0.40.0** (2026-07-27) is required only by SDK v0.55.0; **v1.0.1 (2025-02-03) is a semver trap** — `go get github.com/cometbft/cometbft` resolves to it. Pin `@v0.39.4` explicitly |\n| **Cosmos SDK** | **v0.54.4** (2026-07-28) | v0.55.0 shipped the same day but removes `x/params`, `x/protocolpool`, `SIGN_MODE_TEXTUAL`, forces `x/staking` 5→6 and `x/auth` 6→7, and **protocolpool balances are bank state and are not migrated automatically**. `cosmos/evm` pins v0.54.3, ibc-go v11.2.0 targets v0.54, Ignite still scaffolds **v0.53.6** — re-pin `go.mod` before writing module code. Make v0.54→v0.55 your first *rehearsed* upgrade |\n| **revm** | **pin what reth pins (42.0.1)**; 43.0.0 (2026-08-26) is the upgrade target | 117 versions; v42.0.0 was yanked. Recommending a four-day-old major the largest integrator hasn't adopted maximizes exposure to the churn you're warned about |\n| **jmt** | 0.12.0, **published 2025-10-28** (not 2026-08-16) | One release in ~22 months. **Read-the-source dependency, not a live one.** Ship a sorted-map binary Merkle first (~200 lines); treat JMT as a vendored reference |\n| **rust-libp2p** | umbrella 0.56.0 is **2025-06-27, ~14 months stale** — pin sub-crates (`libp2p-gossipsub` 0.49.5, 2026-07-21) | Sub-crates ship independently |\n| Others | redb 4.2.0 · borsh 1.8.1 · secp256k1 0.33.0 (libsecp256k1 0.8.0) · k256 0.14.0 · ed25519-dalek **3.0.0 (2026-07-06)** · go-libp2p v0.49.0 · `@noble/curves` **2.4.0 published, newest audit is v2.3.0** — the version you install is one minor ahead of the newest audit |\n\n---\n\n# The 12 weeks\n\n---\n\n### Week 1 — Encoding before code · 10 h · all archetypes\n\n**Read.** Bitcoin whitepaper, twice (second pass: find every place it says \"assume\"). yukimotopress, all 6 chapters. Borsh spec — *\"there is a bijective mapping between objects and their binary representations\"*. EIP-2718 (Final).\n\n**Build.** `ENCODING.md` **before any code**: your canonical codec, your nine domain-separation tags (`txid v1`, `sighash v1`, `address v1`, `mt/leaf v1`, `mt/node v1`, `mt/empty v1`, `mmr/bag v1`, `randao v1`, `state-key v1`), and your frozen list. Then a hash-linked list with `verify_chain()`, a hand-written codec (never a serde derive), and a **million-iteration property test**: for all byte strings `b`, either `decode(b)` fails or `encode(decode(b)) == b`.\n\n**Self-check.**\n1. Show the CI job and the seed for the million-iteration codec test. What was the first counterexample it found?\n2. Adding a tenth domain tag later is safe; changing `\"txid v1\"` is a hard fork. Why exactly?\n3. Ethereum's Prague header is 21 fields, three of them vestigial (`ommers_hash`, `difficulty`, `nonce`). What does each cost, per block, forever?\n4. Give the specific ambiguity that disqualifies protobuf for anything you hash, and the specific mechanism that makes Borsh safe. (Hint: unordered containers → *\"ordered in lexicographic order by key\"*; NaN rejected.)\n5. EIP-2718 SHOULD-rule: signatures include the type byte as the first byte of signed data. Construct the attack if you skip it.\n6. Which archetype did you pick? Name the two corpus dimensions now out of scope for you.\n\n**Trap.** Mutating byte 40 of block 3 must fail at exactly height 3 — not height 4, not \"somewhere\".\n\n---\n\n### Week 2 — Crypto by hand, then delete it · 12 h\n\n**Read.** Programming Bitcoin ch. 1–4. BIP-340 (`hash_tag(x) = SHA256(SHA256(tag) || SHA256(tag) || x)` — the tag is doubled so 64 bytes = one SHA-256 block and implementations precompute the midstate). ZIP-215, all four normative rules. SLIP-0010. BIP-350. RFC 9106 §4.\n\n**Build.** Hand-roll `FieldElement`, `Point`, secp256k1, ECDSA, DER, base58check — **then delete it** and switch to `secp256k1` 0.33.0 / `k256` 0.14.0. Ed25519 behind a **ZIP-215-pinned** verifier. Address = `bech32m(hrp, [0u5] ++ convertbits(h(\"address v1\", varint(scheme_id) || pubkey), 8, 5, true))`. Keystore: Argon2id `t=3, p=4, m=64 MiB` + XChaCha20-Poly1305, plus a keystore-v3 exporter.\n\n**Self-check.**\n1. Keypair → address → sign → verify matching a published vector **byte-for-byte**. Which vector? (Use BIP-85's: `m/83696968'/39'/0'/12'/0'` → entropy `6250b68daf746d12a24d58b4787a714b`, mnemonic *\"girl mad pet galaxy egg matter matrix prison refuse sense ordinary nose\"*; and keystore v3 password `testpassword` → secret `7a28b5ba57c53603b0b07b56bba752f7784bf506fa95edc395f5cf6c7514fe9d`.)\n2. keccak256 pads with `0x01`; NIST SHA3-256 pads with `0x06`. Which does Ethereum use, and what fraction of \"my address doesn't match\" bugs is this?\n3. **The corpus's own contradiction — resolve it.** from-scratch-blueprint says *\"use `verify_strict()`\"*; crypto-primitives says `verify_strict()` is not ZIP-215 and pinning ZIP-215 is mandatory. State ZIP-215's equation `[8][S]B = [8]R + [8][k]A` and why the cofactorless form *\"MUST NOT be used\"*. Then split the claim: `ed25519-dalek` **3.0.0** documents ZIP-215 rules for **point decoding** on `VerifyingKey::from_bytes` — that is *not* the same as the cofactored **verification equation**. Which one does your library implement? Write the answer into your spec text. (The chain-split-safe default: pin ZIP-215; `ed25519-zebra` 4.x in Rust, `@noble/curves` with `zip215: true` in TS, wrap Go's `crypto/ed25519`.)\n4. Why does SLIP-0010 (*\"If curve is ed25519 or curve25519: return failure\"* for non-hardened) delete watch-only xpub deposit derivation, and which counterparty refuses you because of it?\n5. Bech32m changed exactly one constant from Bech32: `0x2bc830a3` instead of `1`. What bug did it fix? (Trailing `'p'` + inserted/deleted `'q'`s.)\n6. Two ECDSA signatures share `k`. Write the two lines of algebra recovering `d`. Now explain Milk Sad (CVE-2023-39910): Mersenne Twister seeded with 32 bits of system time, 2,600 wallets, ~$900,000, 29.65 BTC in one sweep.\n\n**Trap.** Never ship encrypt-without-integrity: a wrong password then silently yields a garbage private key and the user sends funds into the void.\n\n---\n\n### Week 3 — Proof of work and difficulty · 10 h · archetype C deep, others shallow\n\n**Read.** jeiwan parts 1–3; naivecoin ch. 2. Bitcoin Core `pow.cpp` and `chain.cpp`. The ASERT (aserti3-2d) upgrade spec. BIP-113, BIP-94, BIP-54.\n\n**Build.** Full 256-bit target. `nBits` compact encode/decode **including the `0x00800000` sign-bit normalization**. ASERT, integer-only, anchored at height 1, with the spec's two edge cases (`next_target == 0 → bits(1)`, `next_target > max_target → max_bits`). MTP-11 floor, FTL = 300 s from **NTP, not network-adjusted time**.\n\n**Self-check.**\n1. Decode `0x1b0404cb`. (bdiff **16307.420938523983**, pdiff 16307.669773817162.) Now encode a target whose top mantissa byte would set `0x00800000`. What must you do?\n2. In ASERT, the exponent uses **truncated** division and `num_shifts` uses an **arithmetic** right shift by 16. Swap them and describe what happens to the curve.\n3. Why is a floating-point ASERT a permanent chain split rather than a rounding bug? Where does `anchor_target * factor` overflow (~2^272 pre-shift) and what do you do about it?\n4. `halflife = N · T · ln 2`. BCH runs 172,800 s at T=600 — what N is that? (**≈415 blocks**, deliberately sluggish because BCH's hashrate is deep.) Compute your halflife for T=120 s and N≈87. (**7,200 s**.)\n5. Explain in three sentences why Bitcoin's 2016-block DAA with the `[T/4, 4T]` clamp kills a small chain.\n6. Which of MTP-11 and FTL bounds the past, which the future? Why did BIP-113 make time-locked transactions take *\"approximately an hour longer to confirm\"*?\n7. Your security budget is **dollars per hour of rentable hashrate on your algorithm**, not market cap. Rounded crypto51 figures: BTC ~$2.1M/hr, Kaspa ~$3.6k/hr, ETC ~$2.8k/hr, BCH ~$8.1k/hr — and crypto51's own methodology **excludes block rewards, which cut the real cost by up to 80%**. So what is the honest net cost to attack a chain at your target hashrate? MIT DCI logged **40+ reorgs of ≥6 blocks** across BTG/HANA/VTC/XVG/EXP/LCC in 2019–2020, with a **>$72,000** BTG double-spend in Feb 2020.\n\n**Trap.** Height-based fork choice. Follow **cumulative work**, always.\n\n---\n\n### Week 4 — Transactions, ledger model, replay · 10 h\n\n**Read.** jeiwan parts 4–6; naivecoin ch. 3–4. Mastering Bitcoin ch. 6. EIP-155 verbatim (`v = {0,1} + CHAIN_ID*2 + 35`, nine RLP elements). Cardano eUTXO docs for one hour, for the contrast: *\"the fees required for a valid transaction can be predicted precisely prior to posting it.\"*\n\n**Build.** UTXO set in an embedded KV store (or the account map, per archetype) — with `COINBASE_MATURITY = 100`. Sighash committing `chain_id` **and** `tx_version`, excluding all signatures and witness data: `sighash = h(\"sighash v1\", u64_le(chain_id) || u8(tx_version) || body)`, separately `txid = h(\"txid v1\", body)`.\n\n**Self-check.**\n1. Three wallets whose balances come from the UTXO set (or state map) — never by rescanning the chain. Prove it by deleting the block bodies.\n2. Demonstrate a transaction valid on chain 1 and rejected on chain 2. What did retrofitting EIP-155 cost Ethereum after mainnet txs replayed on Ethereum Classic?\n3. What invariant relates `COINBASE_MATURITY` to your max reorg depth, and what breaks when maturity < max reorg?\n4. Is the coinbase check `<=` or `==` subsidy + fees? Why?\n5. Why does `int halvings = nHeight / interval; if (halvings >= 64) return 0;` need that guard? (Shifting a 64-bit int by ≥64 is UB.)\n6. Name the two properties UTXO gives you free (locality → parallel verification; outpoint-spent-once → replay protection) and the one accounts give free (wallet and contract simplicity).\n\n**Trap.** Witness data inside the sighash. That's the segwit lesson; pay for it once, in week 4, not at mainnet.\n\n---\n\n### Week 5 — Merkle, reorg, storage schema · 10 h\n\n**Read.** `src/consensus/merkle.cpp` (the comment first). RFC 6962 §2.1 verbatim: `MTH({}) = SHA-256()`, `MTH({d0}) = SHA-256(0x00 || d0)`, and *\"let k be the largest power of two smaller than n\"*. reth's table list. Geth's path scheme + freezer.\n\n**Build.** RFC-6962 transactions root — **promote** the odd node, never duplicate it. Undo log / changesets. `reorg()`: walk both parent chains to the common ancestor, unwind highest-first replaying changesets in reverse, delete `canonical[h]` / tx lookup / receipts, return txs to the mempool, apply forward — **all in one write transaction**, with a `reorg_journal` marker for crash resume.\n\n**Self-check.**\n1. State CVE-2012-2459 precisely. It is *not* \"a duplicated-tx block is accepted\" — such a block is invalid. The bug is that pre-0.6.1 nodes **recorded that block hash as invalid**, which *\"would prevent acceptance of the legitimate block with the same hash\"* — a remote fork/DoS. Severity High, fixed at 100% adoption 2012-05-14.\n2. What is `MTH({})`? How does a 5-leaf tree split? (**4 | 1**, never 2|2|1.)\n3. Why do the `0x00`/`0x01` prefixes stop a 64-byte transaction being reinterpreted as two internal nodes?\n4. Do a 6-block reorg and show the UTXO/state set is **byte-identical** to a genesis replay. Was it one write transaction? Kill -9 mid-unwind 50 times — 50 clean recoveries?\n5. Why must every numeric key be big-endian? What breaks at block 256 if it isn't?\n6. Geth's `--gcmode full|archive` is *\"only relevant in state.scheme=hash\"*. Explain why that sentence proves archive is a **schema** decision, not a flag. (Geth quotes a full archive at *\"nearly 12 TB\"*.)\n\n**Trap.** Shipping without per-block undo data. You cannot reorg, and adding it later forces a full reindex.\n\n---\n\n### Week 6 — P2P · 12 h\n\n**Read.** naivecoin `p2p.ts` (30 min, to see what \"not gossip\" looks like) → libp2p specs: noise (`Noise_XX_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256` only; IK and XXfallback removed), yamux (`/yamux/1.0.0`, **256 KiB default window** — at 80 ms RTT one stream caps near 3 MB/s), gossipsub v1.1/v1.2 → Bitcoin `addrman.h` → `net_processing.cpp` → devp2p `eth/72` (`Status` is now `[vsn, networkid, genesis, forkid, earliest, latest, latestHash]` — **no total difficulty**) and `snap/2` (EIP-8189: `GetTrieNodes`/`TrieNodes` **removed**, `GetBlockAccessLists`/`BlockAccessLists` added).\n\n**Build.** libp2p: QUIC-first (`/ip4/0.0.0.0/udp/P/quic-v1`, ALPN `\"libp2p\"`, TLS 1.3 self-signed cert with OID `1.3.6.1.4.1.53594.1.1`) plus TCP+noise+yamux. **Never offer mplex** — the spec says it *\"is deprecated for applications requiring resiliency and liveness.\"* Gossipsub with **Ethereum's numbers** (D=8, D_low=6, D_high=12, D_lazy=6, heartbeat 0.7 s, `D_out = 2` with `D_out < D_low` and `D_out ≤ D/2`). **Fork digest in every topic string and in the handshake** — `/mychain/ForkDigest/Name/Encoding` — plus a dual-subscribe window of N blocks before activation. Five-node compose; one node serves a 10k-block invalid chain and gets graylisted in <30 s.\n\n**Self-check.**\n1. Run two nodes across an activation height, one upgraded, one not. Show they do **not** share a mesh. Without the fork digest, which gossipsub score component would have made them destroy each other? (**P4, invalid messages.**)\n2. Name the five rust-libp2p gossipsub defaults you overrode and the failure each would have caused: `max_transmit_size = 65536` (your 2 MB block is silently unsendable), `mesh_n_low = 5` (spec says 4), `duplicate_cache_time = 60 s`, `heartbeat_interval = 1 s`, and the default message-id `base58(peer_id) || seqno` (**the duplicate-storm bug**).\n3. What anti-eclipse property does the reserved outbound mesh (`D_out`) buy?\n4. **BIP-152, correctly:** is announce-then-request 0.5×RTT or 1.5×RTT? (The High Bandwidth section says it is *\"the same 1.5*RTT minimum time that nodes take today\"*; the 0.5×RTT figure lives in Implementation Notes and **requires** pushing `cmpctblock` unsolicited right after header validation. Low bandwidth: 1.5×RTT best, *\"at least 2.5*RTT\"* worst.) Which policy did you implement?\n5. addrman buckets on `GetGroup(src)` = /16 or ASN, not IP. What does that do to an attacker's occupancy cost? Recite the constants: 1024 new / 256 tried buckets, size 64, 64 per source group, 8 per address, collision size 10, horizon 30 d, retries 3, max failures 10.\n6. Does Bitcoin Core still have a numeric ban score? (**No** — `PeerManager` exposes only `UnitTestMisbehaving`; misbehaviour is binary discouragement.) So what did you build, and why not accumulating points?\n7. Kademlia: *\"Nodes add another node to their routing table if and only if that node operates in server mode.\"* What one call did you make after AutoNAT confirmed an external address, and what happens if you forget?\n\n**Trap.** An ENR is capped at **300 bytes** (EIP-778). You get a fork digest and a couple of bitfields, not \"arbitrary fields\".\n\n---\n\n### Week 7 — Mempool and fee market (**cluster mempool, not the 2019 design**) · 12 h\n\nThe corpus's own curriculum prescribed ancestor/descendant limits and RBF rules 1–5 here. **That design is superseded.** Bitcoin Core **v31.0 (2026-04-20)** shipped cluster mempool: *\"The mempool no longer enforces ancestor or descendant size/count limits\"*, the **CPFP carve-out is removed**, clusters are capped at **64 transactions / 101 kvB**, RBF requires the **feerate diagram be strictly improved**, and `getmempoolcluster` / `getmempoolfeeratediagram` are new RPCs. `DEFAULT_ANCESTOR_LIMIT`/`DESCENDANT_LIMIT` (25/25) still exist in `policy.h` but no longer govern the mempool.\n\n**Read.** `doc/policy/mempool-design.md` and `mempool-terminology.md` (these **replaced** the deleted `mempool-limits.md` — the corpus's 404 was a deletion, not a broken link). `packages.md`: package feerate is total modified fees over *\"the total virtual size of all transactions in the package\"*, `MAX_PACKAGE_COUNT 25`, `MAX_PACKAGE_WEIGHT 404,000 WU`, and each tx *\"always validated individually first\"*. geth `core/txpool/validation.go`. EIP-1559, EIP-4844 §`fake_exponential`, EIP-7918, EIP-7825, EIP-7623.\n\n**Build.** One owning map + the minimum secondary indexes your block builder actually reads, consistent across insert / replace / evict / expire / block-connect / reorg. **Dynamic** min fee: on byte-cap overflow, evict lowest-feerate first and raise `mempoolminfee` to the last-evicted feerate + incremental relay fee. Replacement requires **both** a ≥10% bump on every fee dimension **and** `incremental_relay_fee_rate × size` absolute (use **100%** for data-carrying types — EIP-4844 only *recommends* 1.1×; geth's blobpool chose 2×). Exponential base fee over one cumulative `excess` counter. `TX_GAS_CAP = 16,777,216 (2^24)` enforced at **both** mempool and block-validity level.\n\n**Self-check.**\n1. Which release removed ancestor/descendant limits and what replaced them? Show `getmempoolfeeratediagram` output from your own implementation.\n2. Which two BIP-125 rules are **gone** and which four survive? (Gone: 1 and 2. Surviving: 3 absolute fee ≥ sum of originals; 4 fee delta pays the replacement's own bandwidth at the incremental relay feerate; 5 ≤100 conflicting clusters; 6 feerate diagram strictly improved.) Full-RBF has been default since v28.0.\n3. Flood 50k low-fee txs. Show the mempool stays bounded and write out the `mempoolminfee` arithmetic. Explain why two honest nodes will legitimately disagree about relayability, and why your integration tests must not assume otherwise.\n4. Classify and say which may ban a peer: bad signature · nonce too low · intrinsic gas too low · insufficient balance · oversized tx. (**Never ban for nonce or balance** — those are transient; the same tx may be valid next block.)\n5. Up 12.5% then down 12.5% under EIP-1559 does not return to start. Show the arithmetic (`base_fee_delta = max(parent_base_fee * gas_used_delta // parent_gas_target // 8, 1)`, and note the `max(…,1)` is on the *up* move only). Now redo it with the EIP-4844 exponential rule and show it is path-independent. Constants: `GAS_PER_BLOB 2^17`, target 393,216, max 786,432, `BLOB_BASE_FEE_UPDATE_FRACTION 3,338,477`.\n6. EIP-7918: write the condition (`BLOB_BASE_COST * parent.base_fee_per_gas > GAS_PER_BLOB * get_base_fee_per_blob_gas(parent)`, `BLOB_BASE_COST = 2^13`) under which excess **grows** by `blob_gas_used * (max - target) // max` instead of decaying. Why does a secondary dimension pinned at its floor mean a real bandwidth cost is being consumed unpriced?\n7. Where does geth put signature recovery in `ValidateTransaction`? (**Step 14 of 21** — ahead of intrinsic gas and the min-tip check. Geth's order is *not* cheapest-first.) You put it last behind a txid-keyed LRU validity cache. Justify the deviation.\n8. **The Cosmos-trunk version of this question:** on your stack, is the minimum gas price a *consensus rule* or *per-operator node config*? If node-local, none of the above analysis binds — one operator running at zero makes the chain free to spam. Decide now: consensus-enforced floor (feemarket/globalfee-class module) or written down as advisory.\n\n**Trap.** EIP-1559 prices **flow**; nothing in it prices **stock**. Charge a refundable rent-exempt storage deposit per account and slot. Ethereum's fixed 25,000 gas `PER_EMPTY_ACCOUNT_COST` is a permanent liability sold at a spot price.\n\n---\n\n### Week 8 — Accounts, state commitment, execution · 12 h\n\n**Read.** execution-specs `forks/*/fork.py`, then `vm/`. What silently goes wrong if you invert it?\n7. What sets your block interval under ABCI 2.0 — config or app? (**The app**: `FinalizeBlockResponse` **field 6, `next_block_delay`**, documented as *\"Previously `timeout_commit` in CometBFT config.\"* Advice to \"tune timeout_commit\" is the old mechanism.)\n8. Trust `CheckTx`? The spec: *\"just a weak filter\"*; *\"A Byzantine node need not care about CheckTx; it can propose a block full of invalid transactions if it wants.\"* Where do you re-validate?\n\n**Slashing numbers to internalize (corrected).** Ethereum's `MIN_SLASHING_PENALTY_QUOTIENT` moved **32 (Bellatrix) → 4096 (Electra)** — not 128 → 4096. That's 1 ETH → **0.0078 ETH** on a 32 ETH validator, deliberately cutting the *initial* penalty 128× so honest operator accidents survive, while the correlation penalty still burns ~everything for a coordinated 1/3 attack. Copy the asymmetry. Cosmos SDK defaults are **testing values**: `SignedBlocksWindow 100` means a 60-second blip jails you — ship 10,000+ and `SlashFractionDowntime = 0` for the first year (live Hub: 10000 / 0.05 / 600 s / 0.0001 / 0.05).\n\n**Hard invariant, enforced by nothing in the software:** `checkpoint_interval < evidence_max_age < unbonding_time`.\n\n---\n\n### Week 10 — Adversarial testing and deterministic simulation · 12 h\n\n**Read.** TigerBeetle's simulator writeup (*\"24/7 on 1024 cores… at 1000x speed\"*, network + storage + process faults, catching *\"both logical errors in the algorithms and coding bugs\"*). (b) A **naive reference executor** written from the spec text — BTreeMap state, no caching — run against the production STF on every fixture, fuzz input and simulated block, asserting identical roots **and error codes**. (c) The fault matrix.\n\n| Fault | Mechanism |\n|---|---|\n| Crash-stop / recover | `docker kill -s KILL`, restart from disk |\n| Pause | `docker pause` / `unpause` |\n| Symmetric partition | `docker network disconnect` |\n| **Asymmetric partition** | `iptables -A INPUT -s <peer-ip> -j DROP` inside one container |\n| Delay / loss | `tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 200ms 50ms distribution normal loss 3%` |\n| Clock skew | `LD_PRELOAD=libfaketime.so.1 FAKETIME=\"+7s\"` — **run this specifically across a fork activation height** |\n| Disk full | data dir on a fixed-size tmpfs |\n| WAL corruption | stop, truncate last N bytes, restart |\n| **Byzantine** | compiled-in `BYZ_MODE=equivocate\\|invalid_block\\|silent\\|censor\\|flood` |\n| **Leader-targeted DoS** | derive the proposer schedule, drop traffic to the next 3 proposers in order |\n\n**Self-check.**\n1. Items marked ✓ were verified against primary text.\n\nYour exposure is a function of three switches, not of your consensus algorithm. **Switch 1** (a transferable unit exists) is cheap and unavoidable. **Switch 2** (you take consideration) is expensive and *entirely optional*. **Switch 3** (you accept and transmit others' value) is the criminal-exposure one.\n\n| ID | Pitfall | How it bites | Preventive measure | Address by |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| E1 | **Taking consideration for the token** (switch 2) | Simultaneously flips Howey prong 1, the PMLA notified limb on an issuer's offer and sale, s.194S TDS falling on **your buyer**, the MiCA white-paper duty, and a FEMA problem with no clean route | Ship a gas token distributed only as validator/block rewards plus a genuinely free claim. Fund development with equity or a SAFE **into a company** — never a token sale. Commit a written answer to \"will consideration ever be taken for this token?\" into the empty repo | `C1` |\n| E2 | **Drifting across the operator line** (switch 3) | 31 CFR 1010.100(ff)(5)(i)(A) ✓: money transmission is \"the acceptance of currency, funds, or other value that substitutes for currency from one person and the transmission of… to another location or person by any means\". The (ff)(5)(ii)(A) exemption covers \"**delivery, communication, or network access services**\" — publishing node and non-custodial wallet software sits inside it. A **hosted relayer, a bridge you can pause and drain, or a fee taken out of a flow you route does not.** 18 U.S.C. §1960 ✓ is **5 years**, and §1960(b)(1)(A) applies \"**whether or not the defendant knew that the operation was required to be licensed**\" | Never custody. Never route value for a fee. Retroactively exposes an offer you believed exempt | Write and enforce a comms policy covering every team member and every channel. A free block-reward token otherwise sits squarely in Art. 4(2)(a) (\"automatically created as a reward for maintaining the distributed ledger\"). Note Art. 143(3) CASP transitional cover ran to **1 July 2026** ✓ — no grandfathering left. Titles III/IV applied from 30 June 2024; the rest, including CASP authorisation, from 30 December 2024 | `T−12w` |\n| E4 | **Indian VDA tax mechanics** | s.115BBH ✓: **30%** + 4% cess + surcharge; \"**no deduction in respect of any expenditure (other than cost of acquisition, if any)**\"; loss \"shall not be set off against income computed under any provision of this Act\" and \"shall not be allowed to be carried forward\". Snapshot format drift breaks new-node onboarding silently at every fork. And the integration surface has its own permanent traps: **SLIP-0010 removes watch-only xpub derivation**, so exchanges cannot derive fresh deposit addresses; a Ledger device app now requires **Rust plus a third-party audit by an approved partner** (6–12 months, real money); the chain ID goes to whoever files the PR first, permanently.\n\n**Counter:** a weekly automated cold-machine join from your own published instructions, running in CI, alerting on failure — plus an Integration Guide dry-run against a real custodian before mainnet.\n\n### 4.         "confidence": "high",
        "brief": "## Cryptographic Primitives, Keys, Addresses and Wallets\n\n### The one rule\n\nYou write no field arithmetic. Every primitive a 2026 chain needs (SHA-256, Keccak-256, BLAKE3, secp256k1 ECDSA, BIP-340 Schnorr, Ed25519, BLS12-381, ECVRF) has an audited, maintained implementation. Your real work is *interface design*: one scheme per job, a canonical byte encoding for everything, a domain-separation tag on every hash, an address with a network prefix, and a `scheme_id` hook so you are not married to one curve forever.\n\n### The six decisions\n\n| Decision | Recommendation |\n|---|---|\n| Account signatures | Ed25519, ZIP-215 semantics pinned as normative consensus text. Choose secp256k1 ECDSA (EIP-155 + EIP-2 low-s + ERC-2098) only if MetaMask compatibility is the product thesis |\n| Hash | BLAKE3 `derive_key(context,data)` internally; SHA-256 for the header hash only if an EVM bridge must verify you |\n| Address | Bech32m (BIP-350), own HRP, version byte, 32-byte hash of a typed key envelope |\n| HD derivation | BIP-39 24 words -> SLIP-0010 ed25519, hardened-only, `m/44'/coin'/acct'/0'/idx'` |\n| Randomness | ECVRF over `(prev_epoch_mix || slot)`, RFC 9381 suite 0x04, `validate_key = TRUE` |\n| Post-quantum | Algorithm agility now, ML-DSA later |\n\n### Hash layer: build this first\n\nBLAKE3's `derive_key` mode is domain separation for free. Its README requires the context string be \"hardcoded, globally unique, and application-specific\", formatted `[application] [commit timestamp] [purpose]`. Freeze the full list on day one; changing a tag later is a hard fork. Minimum set: `txid v1`, `sighash v1`, `address v1`, `mt/leaf v1`, `mt/node v1`, `mt/empty v1`, `mmr/bag v1`, `randao v1`, `state-key v1`. Unit-test that no two contexts are equal.\n\nIf you need EVM-verifiable headers, note BIP-340's alternative: `hash_tag(x) = SHA256(SHA256(tag) || SHA256(tag) || x)`. The tag is doubled deliberately: 64 bytes is exactly one SHA-256 block, so implementations precompute the midstate.\n\nNever call Keccak-256 \"sha3\". Ethereum's keccak256 uses padding byte 0x01; NIST SHA3-256 uses 0x06. Different digests. Half of all \"my address does not match\" bugs are this.\n\n### Signatures: pick one, then pin the accept set\n\nEd25519's catastrophe is not the math, it is that RFC 8032 leaves several checks optional, so libraries disagree on which signatures are valid and two nodes fork. ZIP-215 (Final, 2020-04-27) is the only fully deterministic pin. Its normative rules, verbatim:\n\n- Verification equation `[8][S]B = [8]R + [8][k]A`; the cofactorless form \"MUST NOT be used\"\n- \"It is not required that A and R are canonical encodings\"\n- Small-order points are **not** rejected (cofactor multiplication \"admits more solutions, not fewer\")\n- \"S MUST represent an integer S less than l\"\n\nZIP-215's payoff is that single verification and batch verification agree, so a batch-verifying node never disagrees with a serial one. Copy those four bullets into your spec.\n\nLibrary reality (verified 2026-08): **`ed25519-dalek` does not document a ZIP-215 path.** It exposes `verify()` (permits weak keys) and `verify_strict()` (rejects weak keys); neither is ZIP-215, and `verify_batch()` deliberately skips weak-key checks. The ZIP-215 Rust crate is **`ed25519-zebra` 4.x**. In TypeScript, `@noble/curves` defaults to `zip215: true`. Go's `crypto/ed25519` documents only RFC 8032 compatibility with no ZIP-215 statement, so wrap or replace it for consensus.\n\nSizes and costs that drive design:\n\n| Scheme | Pubkey | Sig | Verify | Use for |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Ed25519 | 32 B | 64 B | ~15 us | user txs, validator votes under ~300 validators |\n| secp256k1 ECDSA | 33 B (or recovered) | 64-65 B | ~50 us | EVM compatibility only |\n| BIP-340 Schnorr | 32 B x-only | 64 B | ~50 us | if you want MuSig2/FROST/adaptors at L1 |\n| BLS12-381 min-pk | 48 B (G1) | 96 B (G2) | ~1-2 ms | consensus votes above ~300 validators |\n\nECDSA's `v/r/s` exists only for public-key recovery: `r` discards the y-coordinate, so up to 4 points fit, and a 2-bit recovery id disambiguates. It saves 32 bytes per tx but hard-wires you to secp256k1 forever, because Ed25519, BLS and ML-DSA have no recovery. ERC-2098 packs `yParity` into the top bit of `s`, which is free precisely because EIP-2 forces low-s.\n\nIf you ever add BLS, proof-of-possession is mandatory, with distinct DSTs (confirmed in draft-irtf-cfrg-bls-signature-05): signature `BLS_SIG_BLS12381G2_XMD:SHA-256_SSWU_RO_POP_`, PoP `BLS_POP_BLS12381G2_XMD:SHA-256_SSWU_RO_POP_`. Without it, an attacker registering `pk_evil = pk_target^-1 + pk_own` forges aggregates the target never signed.\n\n### Merkle structures: three different jobs\n\n**Tx/receipt roots: RFC 6962, verbatim.** `MTH({}) = SHA-256()`, `MTH({d0}) = SHA-256(0x00 || d0)`, and for n>1 \"let k be the largest power of two smaller than n... `MTH(D[n]) = SHA-256(0x01 || MTH(D[0:k]) || MTH(D[k:n]))`\". So a 5-leaf tree splits 4|1, never 2|2|1. The 0x00/0x01 prefixes are what stop a 64-byte transaction being reinterpreted as two internal nodes.\n\nNever pad by duplicating the last node. Precise history: CVE-2012-2459 (2012-05-14) was not that a duplicated-tx block is *accepted* with the same root; such a block is invalid. The bug was that pre-0.6.1 nodes **recorded that block hash as invalid**, which \"would prevent acceptance of the legitimate block with the same hash\" - a remote fork/DoS. Severity High, fix at 100% adoption.\n\n**Header history: MMR.** Append-only, left-packed perfect trees, O(1) amortized append, O(log n) proofs, nothing rewritten. Grin's docs confirm 11 leaves produce 19 nodes. One detail the survey missed: Grin bags peaks \"iteratively from the right, using the total size of the MMR as prefix\" - include the size in the bagging hash or two different-size MMRs can collide. Never use an MMR for mutable state; it cannot delete.\n\n**State: binary sparse Merkle tree** keyed by `h(\"state-key v1\", addr)`, with precomputed default-subtree hashes and a 256-bit sibling bitmap for compression. You need non-inclusion proofs (\"this account does not exist\"); Ethereum's hexary MPT gives shallower trees but is the single largest source of client complexity. Do not copy it.\n\n### Addresses\n\nBech32m's only change from Bech32 is the final XOR constant: `0x2bc830a3` instead of `1`, fixing a real bug where \"whenever the final character is a 'p', inserting or deleting any number of 'q' characters immediately preceding it does not invalidate the checksum\". Bitcoin uses Bech32 for witness v0 and Bech32m for v1-16; a new chain with a version symbol should use Bech32m everywhere.\n\nConcretely: `addr = bech32m(hrp, [0u5] ++ convertbits(h(\"address v1\", key_envelope), 8, 5, true))` with `key_envelope = varint(scheme_id) || pubkey`. HRP `xyz` mainnet, `txyz` testnet, `rxyz` regtest. Emit lowercase, reject mixed case, reject foreign HRP, reject version != 0. Result is 63 chars, inside the 90-char limit. Use a full 32-byte hash: 20-byte addresses give only 2^80 collision resistance, which is marginal for multi-party constructions where an adversary grinds both sides.\n\n### HD wallets\n\nSLIP-0010 is not optional for Ed25519. Master: `I = HMAC-SHA512(Key = \"ed25519 seed\", Data = seed)`, and every 32-byte string is a valid key so the retry loop never fires. Child: `I = HMAC-SHA512(Key = c_par, Data = 0x00 || ser256(k_par) || ser32(i))`, child key is `I_L` directly, no modular addition. Non-hardened is explicitly refused: \"If curve is ed25519 or curve25519: return failure\". Public keys serialize as `0x00 || ENC(x,y)`.\n\nThe cost is real: **no watch-only xpub address generation.** Exchanges cannot derive fresh deposit addresses from an xpub alone. If that is business-critical, take secp256k1 with real BIP-32 - and heed BIP-32's own note that \"knowledge of a parent extended public key plus any non-hardened private key descending from it is equivalent to knowing the parent extended private key\".\n\nSLIP-0044 (status Active) will register a coin type only \"if there is a wallet implementing BIP-0044 for desired coin\", so pick a candidate index, isolate it behind one constant, and expect to change it once. Ship BIP-85 too: `HMAC-SHA512(key=\"bip-entropy-from-k\", msg=k)` at `m/83696968'/39'/0'/12'/0'` must produce entropy `6250b68daf746d12a24d58b4787a714b` and mnemonic \"girl mad pet galaxy egg matter matrix prison refuse sense ordinary nose\". Use that as your CI vector.\n\n### Key storage\n\nNative format: Argon2id + XChaCha20-Poly1305, AEAD tag replacing a separate MAC. RFC 9106's *second* recommended option is `t=3, p=4, m=2^16 (64 MiB), 128-bit salt, 256-bit tag`; its *first* is `t=1, p=4, m=2^21 (2 GiB)`. Use the second for a laptop wallet (~0.3-0.5 s), the first for cold storage.\n\nShip a keystore v3 exporter anyway: scrypt `n=262144, r=8, p=1, dklen=32`, `aes-128-ctr` keyed by `DK[0..16]`, `MAC = KECCAK(DK[16..32] || ciphertext)`. Validate against the published vector: password `testpassword`, secret `7a28b5ba57c53603b0b07b56bba752f7784bf506fa95edc395f5cf6c7514fe9d`. Never ship encrypt-without-integrity: a wrong password then silently yields a garbage private key and the user sends funds into the void.\n\n### Randomness and leader election\n\nRFC 9381 suite 0x04 (ECVRF-EDWARDS25519-SHA512-ELL2). Proof `pi = Gamma || c || s` is **80 bytes** (ptLen 32 + cLen 16 + qLen 32), and `beta` is 64 bytes. Run verify with `validate_key = TRUE`: only then does the VRF \"additionally satisfy full collision resistance and unpredictability under malicious key generation\".\n\nSign over `prev_epoch_mix || u64_be(slot)`, not the epoch number. Plain RANDAO is a deterministic signature over the epoch, so a proposer knows its own contribution far in advance and can withhold a slot to grind. EIP-7998 (Draft, created 2025-08-03) fixes exactly this by signing `RandaoRevealSeed{previous_mix, slot}`. Pair it with a missed-proposal penalty; withholding remains possible even with a VRF. Do not architect around a VDF - none is in production.\n\nUse a separate VRF keypair. Account key, VRF key, P2P identity key and consensus vote key must all be distinct.\n\n### Post-quantum: agility, not ML-DSA\n\nVerified sizes: ML-DSA-44 pk **1312 B**, sig **2420 B**; ML-DSA-65 1952/3293; ML-DSA-87 2592/4595. SLH-DSA is worse than commonly quoted: 128s sig 7856 B, 128f 17088 B, 256s **29792 B**. FIPS 204 was published 2024-08-13.\n\nAt ~40x an Ed25519 signature, shipping ML-DSA at genesis multiplies bandwidth, state and DoS surface for a threat that does not exist yet. Ship instead: (1) addresses are hashes of a typed key envelope so public keys stay hidden until first spend; (2) `varint scheme_id` in both key and signature envelopes, with `0x10` ML-DSA-44, `0x11` ML-DSA-65, `0x20` SLH-DSA reserved and consensus-rejected until a fork activates them; (3) a `tx_version` byte inside the sighash; (4) optional per-account PQ recovery commitment `H(future_pq_pubkey)`. Hashes only lose half their bits to Grover, so BLAKE3-256 stays at ~128-bit security and needs no change.\n\n### Sighash and canonical encoding\n\n`sighash = h(\"sighash v1\", u64_le(chain_id) || u8(tx_version) || body)` where `body` excludes all signatures and witness data. Separately `txid = h(\"txid v1\", body)`. Chain-id inclusion is non-negotiable (Ethereum retrofitted EIP-155 after mainnet txs replayed on Ethereum Classic). Witness exclusion is the segwit lesson.\n\nHand-write the codec. Protobuf, JSON and serde derives all admit multiple encodings of the same message, which makes your txid not a function of your transaction. Property-test that for all byte strings `b`, either `decode(b)` fails or `encode(decode(b)) == b`, for a million iterations, before you write consensus code.\n\n### Library choices (verified 2026-08)\n\n| Language | Choice |\n|---|---|\n| Rust consensus | `secp256k1` **0.33.0** (2026-08-28) binding libsecp256k1 **0.8.0** (2026-08-03; modules schnorrsig, ellswift, musig, silentpayments, extrakeys, recovery); `ed25519-zebra` 4.x for ZIP-215; `blst`; `blake3`, `sha2`, `sha3`; `argon2`, `zeroize`, `subtle` |\n| Rust pure | `k256` 0.14.0 (2026-07-08), NCC-audited (two high-severity findings, since fixed) - but its docs warn it is unsafe on CPUs with variable-time multiply |\n| Go | `blst` Go bindings (NCC Group audit Jan 2021, Galois formal verification ongoing); cgo to libsecp256k1; wrap `crypto/ed25519` |\n| TS/JS | `@noble/curves` (audits: Trail of Bits Feb 2023 v0.7.3, Kudelski Sep 2023 v1.2.0, Cure53 Sep 2024 v1.6.0, Trail of Bits Aug 2026 v2.3.0), `@scure/bip32`, `@scure/bip39`, `@scure/base` |\n\nnoble's README is blunt: \"JIT-compiler and Garbage Collector make constant time extremely hard... any other JS library can't have constant-timeness\", and non-base-point multiplication on ed25519/ed448 is unblinded. Use JS for verification and wallet UX, native audited code for high-value signing.\n\n### The traps that actually drain wallets\n\nMilk Sad (CVE-2023-39910) is the canonical entropy disaster: Libbitcoin Explorer 3.0.0-3.6.0 seeded Mersenne Twister with 32 bits of system time, so `bx seed -b 256` produced 32 bits of real entropy. Over 2,600 wallets affected, ~$900,000 stolen, ~29.65 BTC in one July 2023 sweep. Only ever read the OS CSPRNG.\n\nNonce discipline: two ECDSA signatures sharing `k` give `d = (s1*k - z1)/r` by algebra; a few biased bits over ~100 signatures give it by lattice reduction. Context strings are frozen at genesis.\npub fn h(ctx: &'static str, data: &[u8]) -> [u8; 32] { blake3::derive_key(ctx, data) }\n\npub const CTX_ADDR: &str = \"mychain 2026-01-01 address v1\";\n\n#[repr(u8)]\npub enum Scheme { Ed25519 = 0x01, Secp256k1 = 0x02, BlsMinPk = 0x03 }\n// 0x10 ML-DSA-44, 0x11 ML-DSA-65, 0x20 SLH-DSA: parsed, then REJECTED until forked in.\n\npub fn key_envelope(s: Scheme, pk: &[u8]) -> Result<Vec<u8>, Err> {\n    let want = match s { Scheme::Ed25519 => 32, Scheme::Secp256k1 => 33, Scheme::BlsMinPk => 48 };\n    if pk.len() != want { return Err(Err::BadLen); }        // exact length, no slack\n    let mut v = vec![s as u8]; v.extend_from_slice(pk); Ok(v)\n}\n\npub fn address(env: &[u8], hrp: &str) -> String {\n    let digest = h(CTX_ADDR, env);                          // 32 B, NOT 20 -- 2^128 not 2^80\n    let mut d = vec![u5::try_from_u8(0).unwrap()];          // version symbol\n    d.extend(digest.to_base32());\n    // Variant::Bech32m => final XOR 0x2bc830a3, fixing the trailing-'p'/inserted-'q' bug\n    bech32::encode(hrp, d, bech32::Variant::Bech32m).unwrap()\n}"

        "brief": "## Ledger model, block/transaction structure, state storage\n\nThis is the layer you cannot cheaply change later: it fixes your transaction format, your state commitment, your storage schema, your light-client story, and whether parallel execution is ever possible. Everything below is checked against the spec or source file, not against blog posts.\n\n### 1. Ledger model: UTXO, accounts, eUTXO, objects\n\n**UTXO** (Bitcoin) makes state a set of immutable outputs. A tx names outpoints (32-byte txid + 4-byte index = 36 bytes) as inputs, destroys them, creates outputs. Validity is *local* — it depends only on the tx and its inputs — so replay protection is free (an outpoint is spendable once), verification of non-conflicting txs parallelizes trivially, and the state store is a flat KV set: Bitcoin Core's `chainstate/` is a plain LevelDB of UTXOs with **no trie at all**, and there is no state root in the 80-byte header.\n\n**Accounts** (Ethereum) make state a mutable map `keccak256(address) -> rlp([nonce, balance, storageRoot, codeHash])`. Far simpler for wallets and contracts; costs you an explicit nonce and makes every state access a random read into an authenticated map.\n\n**eUTXO** (Cardano) keeps locality and adds contract state: outputs \"can carry (almost) arbitrary data in addition to an address and value\", and scripts see the datum, the transaction, and redeemers. The payoff, stated by Cardano's own docs: \"the fees required for a valid transaction can be predicted precisely prior to posting it,\" and validation \"depends only on the transaction itself and its inputs.\" The cost is contention — each output is spent by exactly one input, so a shared contract UTXO becomes a global lock.\n\n**Objects** (Sui): every object carries a 32-byte ID (derived from the creating tx digest + counter), an 8-byte monotonically increasing version, the 32-byte digest of the last tx that produced it, and a 32-byte owner, across five ownership classes (address-owned, immutable, consensus-address-owned/Party, shared, wrapped).\n\n**Recommendation: account model.** `Account { nonce: u64, balance: u128, code_hash: [u8;32], storage_root: [u8;32] }`, replay protection via monotonic nonce plus `chain_id` inside the signing domain. Pick UTXO only if privacy or Bitcoin compatibility is a hard product requirement.\n\n### 2. Typed transaction envelope — do this on day one\n\nEIP-2718 (Final): `TransactionType || TransactionPayload`, where TransactionType is \"a positive unsigned 8-bit number between `0` and `0x7f`\"; legacy RLP txs are disambiguated because they start in `[0xc0, 0xfe]`; `0xff` is \"reserved for future use as an extension sentinel value.\" Two rules matter more than the rest:\n\n- Signatures **SHOULD** \"include the `TransactionType` as the first byte of the signed data.\" Skip this and a type-0 signature may validate as a type-1 tx with different semantics.\n- \"the `TransactionType` of the receipt **MUST** match the `TransactionType` of the transaction with a matching `Index`.\"\n\nOne byte bought Ethereum four live types years later: `0x01` access lists (EIP-2930, Final; `[[{20 bytes},[{32 bytes}...]]...]`, 2400 gas/address, 1900 gas/storage key), `0x02` dynamic fee, `0x03` blobs (EIP-4844, Final; network wrapper `rlp([tx_payload_body, blobs, commitments, proofs])`), `0x04` set-code (EIP-7702, Final; authorization tuple `[chain_id, address, nonce, y_parity, r, s]`, `MAGIC = 0x05`, designator `0xef0100 || address`). Ship exactly one type in v1.\n\nFee market: use EIP-1559 from the start. `INITIAL_BASE_FEE = 1000000000`, `BASE_FEE_MAX_CHANGE_DENOMINATOR = 8`, `ELASTICITY_MULTIPLIER = 2`, and `base_fee_per_gas_delta = max(parent_base_fee * gas_used_delta // parent_gas_target // 8, 1)` — floor division, integers only. `priority = min(max_priority_fee, max_fee - base_fee)`, `effective = priority + base_fee`. Retrofitting this invalidates every wallet and fee estimator.\n\n### 3. Header design\n\nBitcoin's header is exactly 80 bytes: version(4) ‖ prev hash(32) ‖ merkle root(32) ‖ time(uint32) ‖ nBits(4) ‖ nonce(4). Ethereum's Prague header (execution-specs `blocks.py`) is **21 fields** — including three vestigial ones (`ommers_hash`, `difficulty`, `nonce`) it will carry forever. Every field is a permanent tax.\n\n| Field | Type | Why it must exist |\n|---|---|---|\n| `parent_hash` | `[u8;32]` | chain linkage |\n| `height` | `u64` | index, fork comparison |\n| `timestamp_ms` | `u64` | never `u32` seconds — Bitcoin's field overflows in 2106 |\n| `state_root` | `[u8;32]` | turns divergence into an immediate halt |\n| `transactions_root` | `[u8;32]` | body commitment |\n| `receipts_root` | `[u8;32]` | provable events for bridges/indexers |\n| `gas_limit`, `gas_used` | `u64` | resource accounting |\n| `base_fee_per_gas` | `u128` | EIP-1559 |\n| `proposer` | `Address` | rewards |\n| `extra_data` | `Bytes`, **cap 32 in validation** | otherwise it becomes free permanent storage |\n| `consensus_seal` | `Bytes` | signature/PoW |\n\nOmit the 2048-bit logs bloom: it costs 256 bytes per header *and* per receipt forever, saturates on busy blocks, and a local KV log index (`address ‖ topic0 ‖ be_u64(block) ‖ be_u32(idx)`) is exact and faster. EIP-7685's `requests_hash` shows the cheap way to add a future commitment: hash each non-empty item, order by type byte ascending, `sha256` the concatenation, `sha256(\"\")` when empty.\n\n**Merkle root — the one place a naive implementation is insecure.** Bitcoin's rule is \"If there are an odd (non-even) number of TXIDs, the last TXID is concatenated with a copy of itself and hashed.\" That is CVE-2012-2459 (2012-05-14): \"Block hash collisions can easily be made by duplicating transactions in the merkle tree… This could be used to fork the blockchain, including deep double-spend attacks.\" Domain-separate leaves and internal nodes and **promote** the odd node instead of duplicating it.\n\n### 4. Canonical encoding\n\nYour block hash, tx hash and state root are hashes of encoded bytes. If two encoders disagree by one byte, the chain splits.\n\n| Format | Determinism mechanism | Verdict |\n|---|---|---|\n| Borsh | \"there is a bijective mapping between objects and their binary representations\"; LE ints, `u32` length prefix, declaration-order fields, `u8` enum ordinal, unordered containers \"ordered in lexicographic order by key\", NaN rejected | **Pick this in Rust** |\n| SSZ | \"designed to be deterministic and also to Merkleize efficiently\"; fixed fields inline LE, variable fields replaced by offsets with data on a trailing heap; generalized index = `2**depth + index in row` | Pick if light-client field proofs are a goal |\n| SCALE | fixed-width LE + compact ints keyed by the low 2 bits (`0`→`0x00`, `1`→`0x04`, `65535`→`0xfeff0300`); \"not self-describing\" | Equivalent to Borsh |\n| RLP | leading-zero integers \"must be treated as invalid\"; 55-byte threshold at `0x80/0xb7/0xc0/0xf7` | Proven, schemaless, merkleizes badly |\n| CBOR §4.2 | preferred serialization; \"keys in every map MUST be sorted in the bytewise lexicographic order of their deterministic encodings\"; \"Indefinite-length items MUST NOT appear\" | Only if you need self-description |\n| Protobuf / JSON | none | **Disqualified for anything you hash** |\n\n### 5. Authenticated state\n\nEthereum's MPT has four node types (NULL, 17-item branch, 2-item leaf, 2-item extension) plus hex-prefix nibble flags 0–3. You need to understand it to reject it. EIP-6800 (Verkle, Pedersen/Bandersnatch) is now **Stagnant**; the live direction is EIP-7864 (Draft, 2025-01-20), a plain **binary** tree: `internal_node_hash = hash(left_hash || right_hash)`, `stem_node_hash = hash(stem || 0x00 || hash(left_hash || right_hash))`, `leaf_node_hash = hash(value)`, `empty_node_hash = [0x00] * 32`, keys = 1-byte type ‖ 31-byte stem ‖ 1-byte suffix. Its own note: \"The hash function used in the current draft is not final.\" Put your hash behind a trait.\n\n**Recommendation:** define `trait StateCommitment { root, prove, apply }`. Ship a sorted-map binary Merkle first (~200 lines, correct, fine for a devnet), then a JMT-shaped sparse tree over hashed keys — \"a 256-bit sparse Merkle tree with an optimization that any subtree containing 0 or 1 leaf node will be replaced by that leaf node or a placeholder node.\" The `jmt` crate (0.12.0, released 2026-08-16, maintained by Penumbra) is live; note its internal nodes hold 16 children as a compressed 4-level binary subtree. Hash the keys — raw keys let an attacker grind a long shared prefix and inflate depth.\n\n### 6. Storage schema and durability\n\nCopy reth's shape (MDBX today, \"exploring redb as an alternative\"): flat tables for execution, separate trie tables, reverse changesets for everything else.\n\n`CanonicalHeaders: BlockNumber→HeaderHash` · `HeaderNumbers: BlockHash→BlockNumber` · `Headers: BlockNumber→Header` · `BlockBodyIndices: BlockNumber→{first_tx_num,count}` · `Transactions: TxNumber→TransactionSigned` · `TransactionHashNumbers: TxHash→TxNumber` · `Receipts: TxNumber→Receipt` · `Bytecodes: B256→Bytecode` · `PlainAccountState: Address→Account` · `PlainStorageState: Address→StorageEntry` (DupSort) · `HashedAccounts` / `HashedStorages` · `AccountsTrie: StoredNibbles→BranchNodeCompact` · `AccountChangeSets: BlockNumber→AccountBeforeTx` (DupSort, subkey Address) · `StorageChangeSets: BlockNumberAddress→StorageEntry` (DupSort) · `AccountsHistory: ShardedKey<Address>→BlockNumberList` · `PruneCheckpoints` · `StageCheckpoints`.\n\nEncode every numeric key **big-endian** — every ordered KV store sorts bytewise, and LE keys silently break range scans at block 256. Commit **one atomic transaction per block** containing header, body, receipts, state writes, changesets, indices, `canonical[height]`, and the head pointer. Never split the head pointer from the data it points at.\n\nEngines: **redb 4.2.0** (2026-08-17) — pure Rust (no clang/bindgen, which matters on Windows), copy-on-write B+trees, ACID, \"MVCC support enabling concurrent readers and a single writer\", savepoints. **libmdbx** — same shape, production-proven, DupSort multimaps, and (correcting a common myth) \"automatic size adjustment on the fly\", unlike LMDB. LSM engines buy write throughput you don't need at the cost of read amplification you can't afford.\n\n### 7. Pruning, sync, reorgs, genesis\n\nGeth's path scheme keeps exactly one state trie on disk plus \"reverse diffs. Every time a new block is imported, a diff is created which can be used to convert the post-state of the block back to it's pre-state\" — 128 blocks in memory, 90,000 reverse diffs on disk (`--history.state`, default 90000, path-only). `--gcmode full|archive` is \"only relevant in state.scheme=hash\" — that is the primary-source proof that archive is a *schema* decision, not a flag. Geth quotes a full archive at \"nearly 12 TB\". Freezer/ancients move data ≥90,000 blocks back into flat files with O(1) reads and 6-byte index entries; EIP-4444 (Draft) sets `HISTORY_PRUNE_EPOCHS = 33,024`.\n\nState sync: copy `snap`. **This changed since most write-ups**: in snap/2, `GetTrieNodes`/`TrieNodes` (0x06/0x07) are **removed** and `GetBlockAccessLists`/`BlockAccessLists` (0x08/0x09) added. Servers \"must Merkle prove the starting hash (even if it does not exist) and the last returned account\"; soft *byte* limits are used because \"it makes the network traffic more deterministic.\" This requires hashed state to be iterable in key order.\n\nReorgs: store the block *tree*. Walk both parent chains to the common ancestor, unwind highest-first by replaying changesets in reverse, delete `canonical[h]`/`tx_lookup`/`receipts`, return txs to the mempool, then apply forward — all in one write txn, with a `reorg_journal` marker for crash resume. Bitcoin Core's `blocks/revNNNNN.dat` \"Block undo data\" is the same idea in file form (with `blocks/index/` and `chainstate/` as LevelDB, `blkNNNNN.dat` at 128 MiB).\n\nGenesis: a JSON chain spec (`config.chainId`, fork activations, `gasLimit`, `extradata`, `alloc`), a `geth init --datadir data genesis.json`-style command, derived header (`parent_hash=[0;32]`, empty roots, `state_root = commit(alloc)`), and the resulting hash exchanged in the p2p handshake. Use **timestamp-based** fork activation only.\n\n### 8. Parallelism: the 2026 answer\n\nDon't design an object model for this. EIP-7928 Block-Level Access Lists (in peer review, created 2025-03-31) adds a `block_access_list_hash` header field over a list that \"record[s] all accounts and storage locations accessed during block execution, along with their post-execution values\", enabling \"parallel disk reads, parallel transaction execution, parallel state root computation and executionless state updates.\" reth already carries `BlockAccessLists` tables and snap/2 gossips them.             "code": "// Bitcoin: \"If there are an odd number of TXIDs, the last TXID is concatenated\n// with a copy of itself and hashed\" -> CVE-2012-2459. Do NOT do that.\nconst LEAF: u8 = 0x00;\nconst NODE: u8 = 0x01;\n\npub fn merkle_root(items: &[Vec<u8>]) -> Hash32 {\n    if items.is_empty() { return H::hash(&[LEAF]); }          // fixed EMPTY_ROOT\n    let mut level: Vec<Hash32> = items.iter()\n        .map(|b| H::hash(&[&[LEAF][..], b].concat()))          // leaf domain\n        .collect();\n    while level.len() > 1 {\n        let mut next = Vec::with_capacity(level.len().div_ceil(2));\n        for pair in level.chunks(2) {\n            next.push(match pair {\n                [l, r] => H::hash(&[&[NODE][..], l, r].concat()), // node domain\n                [l]    => *l,      // PROMOTE the odd node unchanged.\n                _      => unreachable!(),\n            });\n        }\n        level = next;\n    }\n    level[0]\n}\n// Test: root(txs) != root(txs ++ [txs.last()]) for every N."

None means \"did not exist\" (creation),\n            // Some(rec) for updates AND deletions. Getting this wrong = ghost accounts.\n            cs.insert(&changeset_key(h, k), &borsh(&prev))?;   // key = be_u64(h) || addr\n            hist.insert(k, &push_block(hist.get(k)?, h))?;\n            match new { Some(v) => acct.insert(k, v)?, None => { acct.remove(k)?; } };\n        }\n        w.open_table(HEADERS)?.insert(&blk.hash(), &borsh(&blk.header))?;\n        w.open_table(CANONICAL)?.insert(&h.to_be_bytes(), &blk.hash())?;  // BIG-ENDIAN\n        w.open_table(CHAIN_META)?.insert(\"head\", &blk.hash())?;\n    }\n    w.commit()                                        // single fsync boundary\n}\n// Unwind = read changeset_key(h, ..) range in reverse and write prev values back."

            "code": "// EIP-2718: TransactionType is 0..=0x7f; 0xff reserved; signatures SHOULD\n// include the TransactionType as the first byte of the signed data.\npub struct SignedTx { raw: Vec<u8>, ty: u8, payload: TxV0, sig: [u8;64], rec: u8 }\n\nimpl SignedTx {\n    // ONLY constructor: you cannot build one without the bytes it arrived as.\n    pub fn decode(raw: Vec<u8>) -> Result<Self> {\n        let (&ty, rest) = raw.split_first().ok_or(Err::Empty)?;\n        if ty > 0x7f { return Err(Err::ReservedType); }   // 0x80..=0xfe, 0xff sentinel\n        let Wire { payload, sig, rec } = borsh::from_slice(rest)?;\n        // canonicality: re-encoding must reproduce `rest` exactly, else reject.\n        if borsh::to_vec(&Wire{payload: payload.clone(), sig, rec})? != rest {\n            return Err(Err::NonCanonical);\n        }\n        Ok(Self { raw, ty, payload, sig, rec })\n    }\n    // Hash the bytes we received, never a re-encoding.\n    pub fn hash(&self) -> Hash32 { H::hash(&[&[DOMAIN_TX][..], &self.raw].concat()) }\n\n    pub fn sig_hash(&self) -> Hash32 {                // type byte is INSIDE the signature\n        H::hash(&[&[DOMAIN_TX, self.ty][..], &borsh::to_vec(&self.payload).unwrap()].concat())\n    }\n}\n// Receipts mirror this: receipt.ty MUST equal tx.ty at the same index."

        "brief": "## Proof-of-Work and Nakamoto Consensus\n\n### What you are actually building\n\nNakamoto consensus is three rules:\n\n1. **Validity.** `SHA256(SHA256(header80))`, read as a little-endian 256-bit integer, must be `<= target`, where target decodes from the header's 4-byte `nBits`. Verified verbatim in Bitcoin Core `CheckProofOfWorkImpl`: `if (UintToArith256(hash) > bnTarget) return false;`\n2. **Fork choice.** Follow the branch with greatest **cumulative work**, never greatest height. Per-block work is `floor(2^256/(target+1))`. Bitcoin Core computes it without 512-bit math — note the function is named `GetBitsProof` on current master, not `GetBlockProof`: `return (~bnTarget / (bnTarget + 1)) + 1;`\n3. **Difficulty steering.** A DAA drives observed solvetime toward target `T`.\n\nFinality is probabilistic *and conditional on a bounded attacker fraction*. For a new chain that fraction is not bounded. That single fact drives most decisions below.\n\n### Header and compact encoding\n\n80 bytes, all little-endian: `version(4) ‖ hashPrevBlock(32) ‖ hashMerkleRoot(32) ‖ nTime(4) ‖ nBits(4) ‖ nNonce(4)`. Explorers display the digest byte-reversed; put that reversal in exactly one function.\n\n`nBits`: high byte = exponent, low 3 bytes = mantissa; `target = mantissa × 256^(exponent−3)`. Max target `0x1d00ffff` = `0x00000000FFFF0000…0000` (decimal `486604799`, the same constant the ASERT spec calls `max_bits`). Worked example: `0x1b0404cb` → `0x0404cb × 2^(8×(0x1b−3))` → bdiff `16307.420938523983`, pdiff `16307.669773817162`. Bit `0x00800000` is a **sign bit**: on encode, if the top mantissa byte would set it, shift mantissa right 8 and increment the exponent. Chains have split on that line.\n\n### Decision 1 — the difficulty algorithm (highest leverage)\n\n**Recommendation: ASERT (aserti3-2d), integer-only, anchored at height 1.** It is stateless with respect to recent history — it reads only `(anchor_height, anchor_parent_time, anchor_target)` plus the evaluation block's height and time — so it has no oscillation mode, no error accumulation (a fast stretch is repaid by a slow one against an absolute schedule), and a manipulated timestamp perturbs one block and self-corrects.\n\nThe spec's exact pseudocode (verified on the BCHN upgrade spec page) is in the code sketch. Two subtleties the survey glossed: the exponent uses **truncated division** (`trunc_div`) while `num_shifts` uses an **arithmetic** `shift_right(exponent, 16)` — mixing these up shifts your whole curve; and the spec mandates edge cases `next_target == 0 → target_to_bits(1)` and `next_target > max_target → max_bits`.\n\n**Parameterise it for your size, don't copy BCH.** BCH mainnet uses `ideal_block_time = 600`, `halflife = 172800` (2 days), testnet `halflife = 3600`. ASERT's halflife maps to an EMA window of `N` blocks by `halflife = N × T × ln 2`. BCH's 172800s at T=600 is therefore an **N ≈ 415 block** window — deliberately sluggish because BCH's hashrate is deep. At T=120s pick `halflife = 7200` (2 h, N ≈ 87 blocks); at T=600s pick `halflife = 36000` (10 h, N ≈ 87).\n\n| DAA | Response | Oscillates? | Small-chain verdict |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Bitcoin 2016-block, clamp [T/4, 4T] | frozen between epochs | n/a | **Never.** Rented hashrate mines the epoch cheap, leaves, honest miners face clamped 4× difficulty for weeks |\n| DigiShield (Dogecoin) | per block, 1/8 damping | mild | Acceptable, ~15 lines, slow to recover from hash exit |\n| LWMA-1 (zawy12) | per block, linear weights | mild | Good fallback; N=60/90/150 for T=600/120/60 |\n| **ASERT / aserti3-2d** | per block, absolute schedule | **no** | **Ship this** |\n\nVerified DigiShield source (`dogecoin/src/dogecoin.cpp`): `nModulatedTimespan = retargetTimespan + (nModulatedTimespan - retargetTimespan) / 8;` clamped to `[T − T/4, T + T/2]`. That bounds the **target** to `[0.75×, 1.5×]`, i.e. difficulty to `[0.667×, 1.333×]` per block — not a symmetric ±33%.\n\nVerified LWMA-1: `next_D = avg(D) × T / LWMA(solvetimes)` with `L += i * min(6*T, ST_i)`, floor `if (L < N*N*T/20) L = N*N*T/20`, out-of-order timestamps replaced by `previous_timestamp + 1`. zawy's own warnings: LWMA-2/3/4 are deprecated; \"small coins using a large N can go into oscillations from a big miner and end up with 3-day delays between blocks.\"\n\n### Decision 2 — PoW function\n\n**Recommendation: SHA-256d.** Microsecond verification, a 15-year-audited reference, and the only choice that makes merged mining with Bitcoin possible. ASIC resistance is a treadmill you lose: RandomX is the best-engineered attempt ever made — 2080 MiB fast Dataset, 256 MiB light Cache, an empirically-determined 8:1 fast:light ratio, Argon2d with 3 iterations giving a **3423×** penalty for halving memory, ~450 instructions and 155 multiplications per SuperscalarHash, 8 integer + 12 FP registers, 256-instruction program loops — and Bitmain shipped RandomX ASICs anyway. That is the whole trick.\n\n### Decision 4 — block time, size, orphan budget\n\nDecker & Wattenhofer (2013), verified: over blocks 180,000–190,000 they measured **median 6.5 s, mean 12.6 s**, and \"even after 40 seconds there still are 5% of nodes that have not yet received the block.\" They observed **169 forks in 10,000 blocks = 1.69%**, against a model prediction of 1.78%. Orphan probability ≈ `D/T`; a miner with share `q` loses roughly `(1−q)·D/T` of revenue, so the well-connected lose less and the gap compounds. Coinbase output total must be `<=` subsidy + fees, not `==`. For a tail emission copy Dogecoin's shape: `(500000 * COIN) >> halvings` while `nHeight < 6 * interval`, else flat `10000 * COIN`.\n\n### Miner interface\n\nShip **BIP22 `getblocktemplate` + `submitblock` with long-polling**, and keep Stratum out of the node. BIP22 fields verified: `bits`, `curtime`, `height`, `previousblockhash` (big-endian hex), `version`, `transactions[]` each with `data`/`hash`/`fee`/`sigops`/`depends`/`required`, plus `sigoplimit`, `sizelimit`, `coinbaseaux`, `coinbasetxn`, `coinbasevalue`, `workid`, `longpollid`. `submitblock` returns null on accept, a reason string on reject, or an object mapping merged-mining chains to responses.\n\nStratum V1 (Bitcoin wiki, no BIP): `mining.subscribe` → `[[[\"mining.set_difficulty\", id],[\"mining.notify\", id]], extranonce1, extranonce2_size]`; `mining.notify` params in order — job_id, prevhash, coinb1, coinb2, merkle_branch[], version, nbits, ntime, clean_jobs; `mining.submit(worker, job_id, extranonce2, ntime, nonce)`; plus `mining.set_difficulty` and `mining.set_extranonce`. Reserve BIP320's version bits **13–28, mask `0x1fffe000`** (16 bits) and make your validator ignore them (apply `0xe0001fff` for soft-fork signalling), so stock ASIC firmware works unmodified. Stratum V2 is a second-year project; steal one idea now — the extended extranonce split into *prefix / locally reserved / downstream reserved* and `coinbase_tx_prefix ‖ extranonce_prefix ‖ extranonce ‖ coinbase_tx_suffix`.\n\n### Traps that actually kill chains\n\nHeight-based fork choice; `get_compact` sign-bit normalization; floating-point ASERT (platform-dependent → permanent split); overflow in `anchor_target * factor` before `<< num_shifts` (the product reaches ~2^272 pre-shift — use a wide intermediate or short-circuit to powLimit); Bitcoin's network-adjusted time (peers voting on your clock — drop it, use NTP, set FTL = 300 s); shipping without per-block undo data (you cannot reorg, and adding it later forces a full reindex); maturity shallower than max reorg depth; equality instead of `<=` on the coinbase value; relaying and switching to a second-seen equal-work tip — γ is the entire lever in the selfish-mining threshold **α > (1−γ)/(3−2γ)** (γ=0 → 1/3, γ=1/2 → 1/4, γ=1 → ~0), and Eyal & Sirer's fix is exactly uniform random tie-breaking to pin γ at 1/2.\n\n### Flagged as stale, unresolved, or unfetchable\n\n- **BIP54 is marked Complete, changelog v1.0.0 dated 2026-05-22, but I found no mainnet activation height.** Treat it as specified-not-activated and re-check before relying on it.\n- The BCHN GitLab source (`aserti32d.cpp`) and its `qa-assets` test vectors returned **HTTP 403** to me. I verified ASERT against the published upgrade spec only. Obtain the vectors before launch.\n- The Stratum V2 markdown's version-rolling prose reads \"BIP323 / 24 bits\" in the fetched rendering; BIP **320** itself (verified) reserves **16** bits, mask `0x1fffe000`. Trust BIP320 and check SV2 reference code.\n- The Bitcoin wiki Stratum V1 page does not specify coinbase concatenation, merkle folding, or the prevhash byte order; those come from implementations. Prevhash is transmitted **32-bit-word-reversed** — neither plain BE nor LE. Validate your bridge against a known-good pool before mainnet.\n- `bad-cb-amount` in `validation.cpp ConnectBlock` was not retrievable verbatim in my fetch; the rule (`coinbase value out > subsidy + fees` → invalid) is stated from the surrounding source, not quoted.",
