            "question": "Should you launch a standalone L1 at all, or an L2 / appchain?",
            "options": [
              "Standalone L1 with your own validator set and token",
              "OP Stack L2 settling to Ethereum (op-deployer + op-node + op-batcher + op-proposer)",
              "Cosmos SDK appchain with IBC",
              "Just deploy contracts on an existing chain"
            ],
            "recommendation": "Unless your differentiator IS the consensus or execution layer, do not launch a standalone L1. Ship an OP Stack L2 if you need EVM and Ethereum settlement; ship a Cosmos SDK appchain if you need custom state-machine logic, sovereign governance, and IBC connectivity without writing a bridge. Reserve the standalone-L1 path for the case where you have a genuinely novel consensus, VM, or DA design that cannot be expressed as a rollup — and where you can articulate why in one paragraph without using the word 'ecosystem'.",
            "tradeoffs": "L1 buys you sovereignty (your own fee token, no settlement dependency, no sequencer/DA bill) at the cost of owning a validator set, a security budget, a bespoke bridge (the top losses ever: Ronin $624M, Poly $611M, BNB Bridge $586M, Wormhole $326M), and 24/7 consensus on-call. The L2 path costs you L1 DA fees and a settlement dependency but deletes validator recruitment, genesis ceremony, and bridge design from your critical path entirely. The Cosmos path costs you a validator set but IBC deletes the bridge problem, which is the single most dangerous component. DefiLlama's distribution — 148 of 500+ tracked chains under $1M TVL — is the empirical prior on how the L1 bet resolves."
          },
          {
            "question": "What licence for the node software, the SDK, and any app-layer contracts?",
            "options": [
              "MIT everywhere",
              "Apache-2.0 for node + MIT for client libraries",
              "GPL-3.0 / LGPL-3.0 (the go-ethereum split)",
              "BUSL-1.1 with a 2-4 year Change Date"
            ],
            "recommendation": "Apache-2.0 for the node implementation and all Go/Rust crates; MIT for JS/TS client SDKs and example code; BUSL-1.1 ONLY for a specific app-layer contract whose fee capture you are actively defending, never for the node. Put SPDX headers in every source file (`// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0`), a NOTICE file, and a CONTRIBUTING.md with a DCO sign-off requirement rather than a CLA.",
            "tradeoffs": "Apache-2.0 gives you an explicit patent grant and patent-retaliation clause that MIT does not — meaningful when a well-funded fork appears, and it is what Cosmos SDK and Reth both chose (both fetched). MIT is friendlier for libraries an app developer vendors into a closed-source product; forcing Apache-2.0 on a browser SDK creates pointless legal review friction. GPL/LGPL (go-ethereum's split) is defensible but adds compliance questions for anyone embedding your node in a product, which is exactly the integration you want. BUSL on node software is a category error: no exchange, RPC provider, or institutional validator wants a licence question in their infra stack, and the Change Date is capped at four years from first distribution anyway (fetched SPDX text), so you are trading real adoption for a temporary and unenforceable-in-practice moat. Uniswap's BUSL header (fetched) works precisely because it sits on an app whose fee stream is the thing being forked."

A brand-new chain is not on the list, and getting on it is a business-development negotiation with an enterprise price tag, not a signup. The real trade is how much redundancy you self-fund.         "title": "Reference architecture for a from-scratch chain",

        "brief": "though# Reference Architecture for a From-Scratch Chain\n\n## What you are actually building\n\nA node is a deterministic replicated state machine wrapped in four I/O subsystems. The whole architecture is where you cut four seams so each side is testable alone:\n\n1. **The ABCI seam** — pure state-transition function vs. the consensus/network that feeds it.\n2. **The storage seam** — computing a state root (`stage`) vs. persisting it (`commit`).\n3. **The sans-I/O seam** — the consensus state machine vs. the sockets, timers and disk that drive it.\n4. **The codec seam** — canonical bytes vs. in-memory structs.\n\nEverything else is downstream.\n\n## Decision 1: the ABCI split, as an in-process trait\n\nCometBFT's `abci/types/application.go` (main) defines exactly four method groups: Info/Query; Mempool (`CheckTx`, `InsertTx`, `ReapTxs`); Consensus (`InitChain`, `PrepareProposal`, `ProcessProposal`, `FinalizeBlock`, `ExtendVote`, `VerifyVoteExtension`, `Commit`); State Sync (`ListSnapshots`, `OfferSnapshot`, `LoadSnapshotChunk`, `ApplySnapshotChunk`). Four of those matter on day one: `InitChain`, `PrepareProposal`, `ProcessProposal`, `FinalizeBlock`+`Commit`.\n\nThe spec's asymmetry is the load-bearing part, and it is verbatim:\n\n| Rule | Spec text |\n|---|---|\n| Req. 4 | \"`ProcessProposal` is a (deterministic) function of the current state and the block that is about to be applied.\" |\n| Req. 9 | \"calls to `PrepareProposal`, `ProcessProposal`, `ExtendVote`, and `VerifyVoteExtension` at height h do not modify state\" |\n| Req. 11/12 | `FinalizeBlock` state and tx results \"exclusively depend on prior state and the block\" |\n| PrepareProposal | \"The logic modifying the raw proposal **MAY** be non-deterministic.\" |\n| Commit | state changes \"must never replace the previous state until `FinalizeBlock` confirms that the proposed block was decided and `Commit` is invoked for it\" |\n\n**Recommendation: adopt this boundary as a Rust trait / Go interface inside one binary. Do not pay for a socket.** Ethereum's Engine API is the same idea over a process boundary — and as of the Amsterdam fork doc it is `engine_newPayloadV5` / `engine_forkchoiceUpdatedV4` / `engine_getPayloadV6`, returning `PayloadStatusV1.status ∈ {VALID, INVALID, SYNCING, ACCEPTED, INVALID_BLOCK_HASH}`. That split buys independent client teams; you are one engineer, so you get all its costs (JWT auth, a second supervised process, EL-SYNCING/CL-VALID state bugs) and none of its benefits. The in-process trait is a `Box<dyn BlockExecutor>` and gives you 90% of the value: a replay harness, a fuzz target, and a swappable consensus engine.\n\n**The app_hash off-by-one is spec'd, and you will get it wrong once.** `FinalizeBlockResponse.app_hash` \"is included as the `AppHash` in the next block.\" So `header[N].app_hash` = the hash produced by executing block **N−1**. Genesis: `header[0].app_hash = InitChainResponse.app_hash`.\n\n## Decision 2: do not write consensus\n\n| Option | State (verified Aug 2026) |\n|---|---|\n| **Malachite** (Rust) | Apache-2.0, © 2025 Circle Internet Group. README: \"alpha software under heavy development… has not been externally audited.\" Backs Circle's Arc. 780 ms avg finalization at 100 validators / 1 MB blocks; up to 2.5 blocks/s, 13.5 MB/s (~50k tps). **crates.io is a year stale** — `informalsystems-malachitebft-*` last published 0.5.0 on 2025-08-01 while `main` has moved. Pin a git rev. |\n| **CometBFT** (Go) | **v0.40.0, released 2026-07-27**, ABCI 2.0.0. Trap: `go get github.com/cometbft/cometbft` resolves to **v1.0.1 (2025-02-03)** because Go picks highest semver — you must pin `@v0.40.0`. Cosmos SDK v0.55.0 requires exactly v0.40.0. |\n| **Roll your own** | Study exercise only. The bugs are in round skipping, lock/unlock across rounds, WAL-before-broadcast, equivocation detection and timeout escalation — all silent until they cost you safety or liveness. |\n\n**Recommendation: single-validator PoA through M7, then Malachite (Rust) or CometBFT v0.40.0 (Go).**\n\nMalachite's real `Effect` variants (from `core-consensus/src/effect.rs`) are `ScheduleTimeout`, `CancelTimeout`, `StartRound`, `PublishConsensusMsg`, `RepublishVote`, `GetValue`, `RestreamProposal`, `SignVote`, `SignProposal`, `VerifySignature`, `VerifyCommitCertificate`, `VerifyPolkaCertificate`, `WalAppend`, `Decide`, `ExtendVote`, `VerifyVoteExtension`. Its channel tier uses `pub type Reply<T> = oneshot::Sender<T>` with `AppMsg` variants `ConsensusReady`, `StartedRound{role, reply_value}`, `GetValue{timeout}`, `ExtendVote`, `VerifyVoteExtension`, `RestreamProposal`, `GetHistoryMinHeight`, `ReceivedProposalPart`, `Decided{certificate, extensions, reply: Reply<Next<Ctx>>}`, `GetDecidedValue`, `ProcessSyncedValue`. Copy that shape even if you write your own: `step(Input) -> Vec<Effect>` makes Byzantine scenarios a `Vec<Input>` in a single-threaded test.\n\n## Module decomposition and directory layout\n\nDependencies point one direction. **`consensus` must never depend on `executor` or `state`** — if it needs to, you have broken the ABCI seam.\n\n```\ntypes → codec → crypto → storage → trie → state → executor → mempool\n                                                  ↘ consensus (types+crypto ONLY)\n                                                  ↘ p2p → sync → rpc → node → bin\n```\n\n| Rust | Go | TypeScript |\n|---|---|---|\n| `crates/{types,codec,crypto,storage,trie,state,executor,mempool,consensus,p2p,sync,rpc,wallet,telemetry,node}`, `bin/myl1`, `testing/{e2e,fuzz}` | `pkg/{types,codec,crypto,store,trie,state,executor,mempool,consensus,p2p,sync,rpc,wallet,telemetry}`, `internal/node`, `cmd/myl1`, `proto/` + `buf.gen.yaml`, `test/e2e` | pnpm workspace `packages/{…same…}`, `apps/{node,cli}`, `\"type\":\"module\"`, `tsconfig.base.json` with `strict:true` + project references |\n\nReth is the layout to copy: 32 top-level dirs under `crates/` including `chain-state`, `engine`, `evm`, `net`, `payload`, `stages`, `storage`, `transaction-pool`, `trie`. Its workspace pins `edition = \"2024\"`, `rust-version = \"1.95\"`, `resolver = \"2\"`, `version = \"2.5.1\"`.\n\n## Concurrency: one writer, bounded channels, snapshots for readers\n\nOne task owns committed state. Everything else sends messages over **bounded** `mpsc` with `oneshot` replies and reads `Arc<Snapshot>` at a version.\n\n| Language | The three ways it actually hurts |\n|---|---|\n| **Rust/tokio** (recommended) | (a) a `Mutex`/`RwLock` guard held across `.await` deadlocks the executor — `clippy::await_holding_lock = \"deny\"` in CI; (b) redb/rocksdb/JMT calls are **synchronous** and starve worker threads — route every state read/commit through `spawn_blocking` or a dedicated thread pool, this is the #1 cause of 2-second p95 RPC latency; (c) `tokio::select!` branches are not cancellation-safe — a half-consumed stream in a losing branch silently drops votes. |\n| **Go** | (a) `map` iteration order is randomised — any `range` over a map in the STF is a nondeterminism bomb (the ABCI spec names \"hash-table iteration\" explicitly); (b) goroutine leaks when a channel is never drained — thread `context.Context` everywhere and always `select` on `ctx.Done()`; (c) GC STW spikes past ~10 GB of state cache — set `GOMEMLIMIT`, push caches into Pebble's block cache. |\n| **Node/TS** | The event loop is both the architecture and the ceiling. 1,000 secp256k1 verifications at ~60 µs is a 60 ms stall that blows your propose timeout. Batch-verify in `worker_threads`; `bigint` for all balances/nonces (`number` loses precision above 2⁵³) and accept it is 10–50× slower than `u128`. Fine for wallet/light client/indexer; not for a validator. |\n\n## Verified dependency set (checked on crates.io / npm / proxy.golang.org, 2026-08-30)\n\n| Role | Rust | Go | TypeScript |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Runtime | `tokio` 1.53.1 | goroutines | Node ≥22 |\n| Hashes/curves | `ed25519-dalek` **3.0.0** (2026-07-06), `k256` **0.14.0** (2026-07-08), `secp256k1` **0.33.0** (2026-08-28), `sha2`/`sha3` | `decred/dcrd/dcrec/secp256k1/v4` **v4.4.1** (what CometBFT uses; `btcec/v2` wraps it) | `@noble/curves` 2.4.0, `@noble/hashes` 2.4.0 |\n| Canonical codec | `borsh` **1.8.1** (2026-08-26) or `parity-scale-codec` 3.7.5 | gogoproto + a SignDoc scheme | custom over `Uint8Array` |\n| Wire/RPC codec | `prost` 0.14.4 | protobuf | JSON |\n| Storage | `redb` **4.2.0** (2026-08-17) → `rocksdb` **0.25.0** (2026-08-16) or `reth-libmdbx` | `cockroachdb/pebble/v2` **v2.1.7** (2026-08-24) | `classic-level` 3.0.0 |\n| Commitment | `jmt` 0.12.0 (2025-10-28, low activity — read it, don't just trust it) | `cosmos/iavl` v1.2.8 | hand-rolled SMT |\n| P2P | `libp2p` 0.56.0 (umbrella, 2025-06 — but `libp2p-gossipsub` is **0.49.5**, 2026-07-21; sub-crates ship independently) | `go-libp2p` **v0.49.0** (2026-07-28) | `libp2p` 3.3.9 |\n| RPC | `jsonrpsee` 0.26.0 (what reth pins) | `grpc` v1.83.0 + JSON-RPC gateway | `fastify` 5.12.1 |\n| CLI / logs | `clap` 4.6.6, `tracing` 0.1.44 | `cobra` v1.10.2, `viper` v1.21.0 | commander |\n| EVM (optional, M10+) | `revm` **43.0.0** (2026-08-26); reth still pins 42.0.1 | — | — |\n\n## Numbers that matter\n\n**Gossipsub v1.0 defaults (spec, verbatim):** `D=6`, `D_low=4`, `D_high=12`, `D_lazy=D`, `heartbeat_interval=1s`, `fanout_ttl=60s`, `mcache_len=5`, `mcache_gossip=3`, `seen_ttl=2min` — raise `seen_ttl` above your block time. **v1.1:** `PruneBackoff=1min`, `UnsubscribeBackoff=10s`, `FloodPublish=true`, `GossipFactor=0.25`, `D_score=4–5`, `D_out=2`. Wire your signature verifier to the **P₄ (invalid messages)** score component — that one hookup is your cheapest DoS defence.\n\n**CometBFT `DefaultConsensusConfig()`:** `TimeoutPropose=3000ms`, `TimeoutProposeDelta=500ms`, `TimeoutPrevote=1000ms`, `TimeoutPrevoteDelta=500ms`, `TimeoutPrecommit=1000ms`, `TimeoutPrecommitDelta=500ms`, `TimeoutCommit=1000ms`, `PeerGossipSleepDuration=100ms`. **Mempool:** `Size=5000`, `MaxTxsBytes=1GiB`, `MaxTxBytes=4MiB`, `CacheSize=10000`.\n\n## M0–M10 ladder\n\n| M | Build | Definition of done / demo |\n|---|---|---|\n| 0 | Hash-linked list + `verify_chain()` in a REPL | Mutating block 2 fails at exactly height 3. *(2–4 h)* |\n| 1 | Canonical codec + domain tags + proptest/fuzz | 10 M round-trips clean; same logical value → one unique hash across 1,000 encodings. *(1 d)* |\n| 2 | `Signer`, addresses, signed tx, encrypted keystore | Sig over chain_id 1 fails on chain_id 2; one flipped bit fails. *(1–2 d)* |\n| 3 | `BlockStore` over redb, one write txn per block, head marker last | 50/50 clean recoveries from `kill -9` mid-write. *(1–2 d)* |\n| 4 | `Account{nonce,balance}`, `stage`/`commit`, JMT root, genesis | `stage()` twice → byte-identical root, zero disk writes; `query account --prove` → `proof: VALID`. *(3–5 d)* |\n| 5 | `TxPool` + 1 s block timer + `Transfer` execution | 1,000 out-of-order txs land in nonce order; total supply invariant asserted every block. *(3–5 d)* |\n| 6 | **Replay harness** + CI determinism gate | 10,000 recorded blocks produce identical app_hash in debug, release and aarch64; inserting `Instant::now()` turns CI red. *(2–3 d — highest leverage in the ladder)* |\n| 7 | libp2p: Noise+yamux+gossipsub, topics `/myl1/1/{tx,block}` | Two nodes lockstep for 1,000 blocks; corrupt-block sender graylisted <30 s. *(1–2 wk)* |\n| 8 | Malachite or CometBFT, 4 validators, consensus WAL fsync-before-broadcast | Kill 1 → no halt; kill 2 → halt (prove your voting math); same key started twice → refused by the signer's high-water mark. *(2–4 wk)* |\n| 9 | Block sync + snapshot sync (chunked flat KV @ version + root check) | Fresh node catches up to identical app_hash; a snapshot with one altered account is rejected at root verification. *(2–3 wk)* |\n| 10 | Stake/Unstake/Delegate, validator updates, slashing from `evidence`, jsonrpsee RPC, Prometheus | 7-node testnet, 7 days unattended; double-signer slashed and jailed. *(4–8 wk)* |\n\n## The ten code-level mistakes\n\n1. **Non-canonical encoding on a hashed path** — hash-map iteration, protobuf `optional`/varint ambiguity, JSON key order. One canonical encoder; `BTreeMap` only; sort the write set before hashing.\n2. **No domain separation** — a precommit signature is also a valid transaction signature. Prefix every preimage with a one-byte tag + chain_id.\n3. **Fusing stage and commit** — violates ABCI Req. 9; a rejected proposal poisons the DB unrecoverably.\n4. **The app_hash off-by-one** — works on one node, diverges at height 1 on two.\n5. **Nondeterminism in the executor** — the spec's own four categories: hardware faults; node-dependent state (random numbers, time); underspecification (library versions, race conditions, floating point, serialization, hash-table iteration); external sources (filesystem, network calls).\n6. **Trusting `CheckTx`** — spec: \"just a weak filter\"; \"A Byzantine node need not care about CheckTx; it can propose a block full of invalid transactions if it wants.\" Re-validate everything inside `execute()`.\n7. **Unbounded channels / no backpressure** — a slow consumer becomes an OOM instead of a load-shed signal.\n8. **Sync DB calls on the async runtime** (Rust) — every redb/RocksDB call needs `spawn_blocking`.\n9. **Signing before fsync** — a crash-restart double-signs. Put the (height,round,step) high-water mark *inside* the signer so it survives a DB rollback and a duplicate operator.\n10. **Plain `verify()` for Ed25519** — use `verify_strict()` (it \"performs *both*\" scalar and group-element malleability checks) and write down in your chain spec which you use; a peer whose library accepts what yours rejects is a chain split.",

            "code": "// crates/state — the pure/impure seam. `stage` MUST NOT touch disk (ABCI Requirement 9).\npub trait StateDb: Send + Sync + 'static {\n    type Snap: StateReader + Clone + Send + Sync;\n    fn snapshot_at(&self, version: u64) -> Result<Self::Snap, Error>;\n    fn stage(&self, base: u64, w: &WriteSet) -> Result<(Hash, PendingBatch), Error>; // PURE\n    fn commit(&self, version: u64, b: PendingBatch) -> Result<(), Error>;   // ONE atomic txn\n    fn prove(&self, version: u64, key: &[u8]) -> Result<MerkleProof, Error>;\n}\n\n// crates/executor — this IS your ABCI app. `consensus` depends on THIS, never on `state`.\npub trait BlockExecutor: Send + Sync + 'static {\n    fn init_chain(&self, g: &Genesis) -> Result<(Hash, Vec<ValidatorUpdate>), Error>;\n    /// Deterministic: same (base, input) => same app_hash on every machine and build.\n    /// No Instant::now, no rand, no HashMap iteration, no f64, no I/O. NEVER the only validity check.\n    fn check_tx(&self, base: u64, raw: &[u8], k: CheckKind) -> Result<CheckOk, Error>;\n    /// ABCI PrepareProposal: local block building. MAY be non-deterministic (spec-sanctioned).\n    fn prepare_proposal(&self, base: u64, c: Vec<Bytes>, max_tx_bytes: usize) -> Vec<Bytes>;\n}\n// header[N].app_hash == the hash produced by executing block N-1. CometBFT spec: \"This Merkle\n// root will be included as the AppHash in the NEXT block.\" Never block N's own hash."

            "language": "rust",
            "code": "// crates/consensus — no threads, no sockets, no clock. Byzantine tests are just Vec<Input>.\npub enum Input  { Start{h:u64, vs:ValidatorSet}, Proposal(SignedProposal), Vote(SignedVote),\n                  TimeoutElapsed(Timeout), ValueBuilt(ProposedValue) }\npub enum Effect { PublishConsensusMsg(ConsensusMsg), ScheduleTimeout(Timeout, Duration),\n                  GetValue{h:u64, round:i32, timeout:Duration}, SignVote(Vote),\n                  SignProposal(Proposal), VerifyCommitCertificate(Cert),\n                  WalAppend(WalEntry), Decide(CommitCertificate) }\npub trait ConsensusEngine { fn step(&mut self, i: Input) -> Vec<Effect>; }\n\n// crates/node — the driver. Effect ORDER is load-bearing: WalAppend precedes any publish.\nasync fn drive(&mut self, input: Input) -> Result<()> {\n    for eff in self.engine.step(input) {\n        match eff {\n            // fsync BEFORE broadcast, or a crash-restart double-signs and slashes you.\n            Effect::WalAppend(e) => self.wal.append_and_fsync(&e)?,\n            Effect::SignVote(v) => {\n                let s = self.signer.sign(Domain::Vote, self.chain_id, &v.canonical(), v.hrs())?;\n                self.net.publish(TOPIC_CONSENSUS, s.encode()).await?;\n            }\n            Effect::ScheduleTimeout(t, d) => self.timers.schedule(t, d),\n            Effect::GetValue{h, timeout, ..} => {\n                let txs = self.pool.reap(MAX_BLOCK_BYTES, MAX_BLOCK_GAS);\n                let v = tokio::time::timeout(timeout, self.build(h, txs)).await??;\n                self.queue.push(Input::ValueBuilt(v));   // never hold consensus hostage\n            }\n            Effect::Decide(cert) => self.commit_decided(cert).await?,\n            _ => {}\n        }\n    }\n    Ok(())\n}"

            "label": "Domain-separated canonical hashing, and the anti-double-sign guard living inside the Signer",
            "language": "rust",
            "code": "// crates/codec — ONE canonical encoder; every preimage tagged. A vote must never be a valid tx.\n#[repr(u8)] pub enum Domain { Header = 1, Vote = 2, Proposal = 3, Tx = 4, Evidence = 5 }\npub fn preimage(d: Domain, chain_id: u64, body: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {\n    let mut v = Vec::with_capacity(9 + body.len());\n    v.push(d as u8);\n    v.extend_from_slice(&chain_id.to_le_bytes());\n    v.extend_from_slice(body);            // body = borsh(struct); BTreeMap only, never HashMap\n    v\n}\npub fn hash(d: Domain, chain_id: u64, body: &[u8]) -> Hash {\n    Sha256::digest(preimage(d, chain_id, body)).into()\n}\n\n// crates/crypto — the high-water mark lives HERE, not in consensus. It must survive a consensus\n// bug, a rollback of the node's DB, and an operator running two nodes on one key.\nimpl Signer for FileSigner {\n    fn sign(&self, d: Domain, chain_id: u64, body: &[u8], hrs: Option<Hrs>) -> Result<Signature> {\n        if let Some(new) = hrs {                        // Hrs = (height, round, step), Ord\n            let mut hw = self.hw.lock();                // std Mutex; NEVER held across an .await\n            if new <= *hw { return Err(SignerError::DoubleSign { last: *hw, attempted: new }); }\n            self.state_file.write_all(&borsh::to_vec(&new)?)?;\n            self.state_file.sync_all()?;                // fsync BEFORE the key touches the message\n            *hw = new;\n        }\n        Ok(self.key.sign(&preimage(d, chain_id, body)))\n    }\n}\n// Verification side: always VerifyingKey::verify_strict(), never verify()."
          }

            "tradeoffs": "Rust: the borrow checker is a free consensus-safety property — aliasing bugs on shared state simply don't compile, and `Arc<Snapshot>` makes the immutable-read pattern natural. Cost: 2–3× the initial keystrokes, and async Rust has real traps (below). Go: fastest path to a *working* chain because CometBFT v0.40 + Cosmos SDK give you consensus, p2p, state sync and an app framework on day one; interfaces are trivially mockable; `go test -race` catches real bugs. Cost: GC pauses become the tail-latency story once your state cache is tens of GB, and `map` iteration order is a nondeterminism footgun that has bitten production chains. TypeScript: `@noble/curves` 2.4.0 and `@noble/hashes` 2.4.0 are audited and genuinely good, `libp2p` 3.3.9 is real; but a single event loop means 1,000 secp256k1 verifications (~60µs each) is a 60ms stall that blows your consensus timeout, and BigInt math is an order of magnitude slower than u128."

One `node` task owns committed state; p2p, mempool, RPC, and consensus are separate tasks communicating over bounded `mpsc` channels with `oneshot` reply senders (exactly Malachite's `Reply<T> = oneshot::Sender<T>` shape). Readers get `Arc<Snapshot>` at a version and never block the writer.",
            "tradeoffs": "Language-specific failure modes you must design around. **Rust/tokio**: (a) holding a `Mutex`/`RwLock` guard across `.await` deadlocks the executor — enforce with `clippy::await_holding_lock` denied in CI; (b) redb/rocksdb/JMT calls are *synchronous* and will starve the tokio worker — every state read or commit must go through `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` or a dedicated `std::thread` pool, and forgetting this is the #1 reason a Rust node's p95 RPC latency is 2 seconds; (c) `tokio::select!` branches are not cancellation-safe by default — a half-consumed stream in a losing branch silently drops messages, which in a consensus loop means dropped votes; (d) unbounded channels turn a slow consumer into an OOM. **Go**: (a) goroutine leaks when a channel is never drained on shutdown — thread `context.Context` through every send/receive and always `select` on `ctx.Done()`; (b) map iteration order is randomised, so any `range` over a map in the STF is a nondeterminism bomb — sort keys, and run `go test -race` in CI unconditionally; (c) GC STW spikes appear once your state cache passes ~10GB — set `GOMEMLIMIT` and push caches off-heap into Pebble's block cache; (d) unbuffered channels hide backpressure until they deadlock. **Node/TS**: the event loop is the architecture and it is also the ceiling — hashing and signature verification are CPU-bound and will stall consensus, so batch-verify inside `worker_threads` (or a native addon) and keep the main loop for I/O only; there is no shared-memory state between workers except `SharedArrayBuffer`, so the actor model is actually *easier* to express, but you cannot execute blocks in parallel and `BigInt` arithmetic is 10–50× slower than native u128, so gas accounting and balance math become a measurable fraction of block time."

            "question": "What RPC surface and framework?",
            "options": [
              "JSON-RPC over HTTP+WS (jsonrpsee 0.26.0 / fastify 5.12.1 / net-rpc)",
              "gRPC (grpc-go v1.83.0 / tonic)",
              "REST",
              "GraphQL"
            ],
            "recommendation": "JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP and WebSocket as the primary surface — `jsonrpsee` 0.26.0 in Rust, `grpc` + a JSON-RPC gateway in Go, `fastify` 5.12.1 in TypeScript. Add gRPC only for node-to-node/internal tooling.",
            "tradeoffs": "JSON-RPC is what every wallet, block explorer, and indexer in existence already speaks; picking anything else means writing your own client libraries in four languages. jsonrpsee is what reth ships (0.26.0 in its workspace) and gives you server, client, WS subscriptions, and proc-macro-defined API traits — define your RPC as a trait so the client is generated and stays in sync. Version caveat: crates.io currently reports jsonrpsee `max_stable_version` 0.26.0 (Aug 2025) while a 0.24.11 maintenance backport was published later (May 2026) — take 0.26.0, which is what reth uses. gRPC is better-typed and faster but browsers can't call it without a proxy and no wallet speaks it. GraphQL is a poor fit for a chain's query patterns (you want `getBlockByNumber`, not a resolver graph). Design your method names to shadow Ethereum's (`chain_getBlockByNumber`, `chain_sendRawTransaction`) even if your chain isn't EVM — tooling authors will thank you."
          },
          {
            "question": "Where does the validator's signing key live?",
            "options": [
              "In the node process, loaded from a file at startup",
              "In a separate signer process behind a socket (remote signer)",
              "HSM / KMS",
              "Threshold signing"
            ],
            "recommendation": "Design the `Signer` trait from day one (`fn public_key(&self) -> PublicKey; fn sign(&self, domain: Domain, msg: &[u8]) -> Signature`) with a file-backed impl for M0–M9 and a socket-backed remote-signer impl at M10. Put the double-sign guard (last-signed height/round/step, fsync'd) *inside the signer*, not in consensus.",
            "tradeoffs": "In-process is simplest and is fine for a devnet. But the moment you have real stake, key compromise = total loss and double-signing = slashing, and both are handled by the same abstraction. Putting the anti-double-sign state inside the signer is the key insight: it survives a consensus bug, a rollback of the node's DB, and a rogue operator running two nodes with the same key — which is by far the most common way validators get slashed in practice. The trait costs you nothing now and is unretrofittable later because consensus will have grown twelve call sites that sign raw bytes."
          },
          {
            "question": "How do I get confidence in determinism before I have a network?",
            "options": [
              "Multi-node integration tests only",
              "Deterministic replay harness + differential fuzzing on the executor",
              "Formal spec (Quint/TLA+)",
              "Property tests on the state machine"
            ],
            "recommendation": "Build a replay harness at M6, before you build p2p. It reads a file of `(base_version, ExecInput)` records, runs `execute()`, and asserts the `app_hash` sequence matches a golden file. Wire it into CI on every commit, and add a `cargo-fuzz` target that feeds arbitrary bytes to your decoder and arbitrary tx sequences to `execute()`.",
            "tradeoffs": "Multi-node tests find nondeterminism only if the divergence happens to trigger in the 5 minutes your test runs, and then give you a useless error ('app hash mismatch') hours of log-diffing from a cause. The replay harness turns that into a one-command bisect: run the golden stream under both binaries, diff the first differing height, dump the write set. It costs about 150 lines. Differential fuzzing (run the same input through two builds — debug vs release, x86 vs ARM — and diff the roots) catches the platform-dependent class (float, unaligned reads, `usize` width) that nothing else will. Formal specs are genuinely valuable for the consensus core specifically — Malachite's Quint models are why its state machine is trustworthy — but for a solo builder the ROI on specifying your *executor* is low; spend that time on the fuzz target."
          }
        ],
        "pitfalls": [
          "1. NON-CANONICAL ENCODING ON A HASHED PATH. Symptom: two honest nodes compute different block hashes for the same block; the chain forks or halts at a random height. Causes: iterating a `HashMap`/Go `map` into a hash; protobuf's optional-field and varint ambiguity; JSON with unordered keys; float formatting; omitting vs. writing a zero-length optional. Fix: exactly one canonical encoder (borsh 1.8.1 or SCALE 3.7.5) for everything you hash or sign; `BTreeMap` only; sort your write set by key before committing it to the tree; and a proptest that encodes the same logical value 1,000 times asserting one unique output. Protobuf is fine on the wire and dangerous in a preimage — Cosmos had to invent SignDoc precisely because of this.",
          "2. HASHING WITHOUT DOMAIN SEPARATION. Symptom: a validator's precommit signature is also a valid signature over a transaction that drains its account, or a vote for round 3 replays as a vote for round 7. Cause: signing `sha256(borsh(msg))` with no type tag and no chain_id. Fix: every signed or hashed preimage starts with a one-byte domain tag and the chain_id: `sha256(0x02 ‖ chain_id_le ‖ height_le ‖ round_le ‖ borsh(vote))`. Write a test that constructs a Vote and a Transaction that borsh-encode to the same bytes and asserts their hashes differ. This is a 30-minute fix that prevents a total-loss bug.",
          "3. FUSING STAGE AND COMMIT — writing state during proposal validation. Symptom: a node that rejected a proposal, or crashed between prevote and commit, has state it cannot roll back and cannot re-derive; it halts on restart with an app_hash mismatch. Cause: `process_proposal` calling `state.apply(writes)` instead of `state.stage(writes)`. The ABCI spec is explicit — requirement 9 says calls to PrepareProposal/ProcessProposal/ExtendVote/VerifyVoteExtension MUST NOT modify the committed state. Fix: `stage()` returns `(root, PendingBatch)` and touches nothing; `commit()` is the only method that writes; make `stage` take `&self` on a read-only handle so the compiler enforces it.",
          "4. THE APP_HASH OFF-BY-ONE. Symptom: everything works on a single node and every multi-node setup diverges at height 1. Cause: putting the app_hash *resulting from* executing block N into block N's own header — which is impossible, since the header must be hashed before execution. Fix: `header[N].app_hash = app_hash after executing block N-1`, exactly as CometBFT does (`FinalizeBlockResponse.app_hash` is included as `Header.AppHash` in the next block). Genesis: `header[0].app_hash = InitChainResponse.app_hash`. Write this in a comment above the field, because you will second-guess it three times.",
          "5. NONDETERMINISM SMUGGLED INTO THE EXECUTOR. Symptom: nodes agree for weeks, then diverge on one block, and the block looks completely ordinary. Causes, in descending order of frequency: reading the wall clock (`Instant::now()`, `time.Now()`, `Date.now()`) instead of `header.time_ms`; unseeded `rand`; iterating a hash map; `f64` anywhere in fee/reward math; `usize`/`int` width differing between a 32-bit and 64-bit node; unspecified integer overflow behaviour differing between debug and release builds in Rust; a `HashSet` used for dedup where insertion order leaks into output. Fix: the M6 replay harness comparing debug vs release vs aarch64 on every commit, plus banning `std::time`, `rand`, and `HashMap` from the executor crate with a `#![deny]` / import-lint. CometBFT's app-requirements spec enumerates exactly this list — treat it as a checklist.",
          "6. NON-ATOMIC COMMIT. Symptom: after any `kill -9`, OOM, or spot-instance reclaim, the node starts with a block written but its state batch missing (or vice versa) and refuses to start, or worse, starts with silently wrong state. Cause: separate write batches for block bytes, certificate, state, and the head marker. Fix: one transaction containing all four, with the head-height marker written last *inside* it; on startup, read the marker and treat anything above it as absent. Then actually test it: a loop that SIGKILLs the node at a random microsecond of every block for 200 blocks and asserts clean recovery each time. Do this at M3, when the storage layer is 200 lines, not at M9 when it is 3,000.",
          "7. TRUSTING CHECKTX / THE MEMPOOL AS A VALIDITY GATE. Symptom: a hand-crafted transaction that never entered any mempool is included by a Byzantine (or just buggy) proposer and applies with a negative balance, a reused nonce, or an invalid signature. Cause: validating signature/nonce/balance in the mempool path and skipping it in `execute` 'because it was already checked'. The ABCI spec states plainly that CheckTx is 'a weak filter' and that a Byzantine proposer can include arbitrary transactions. Fix: `execute()` re-validates everything, unconditionally, and treats an invalid tx as a *failed* tx (deterministic error result) rather than a panic. Bonus fix: make `check_tx` literally call the same validation function as `execute`, with a flag for the cheap subset.",
          "8. SIGNATURE MALLEABILITY AND MISSING REPLAY BINDING. Symptom (malleability): the same logical transaction exists under two different tx hashes; your tx index, your nonce dedup, and your users' UX all break. Symptom (replay): a transaction signed on your testnet is valid on your mainnet, or a transaction from your chain is valid on a fork. Causes: accepting high-s ECDSA signatures without normalising to low-s; not binding chain_id (and ideally a genesis hash) into the signed preimage; computing the tx hash over the signature-inclusive bytes. Fix: for secp256k1, reject or normalise high-s at the boundary (`k256` 0.14.0 / `secp256k1` 0.33.0 both expose this); include chain_id in the preimage; compute the tx id over the *body* if you want signature-independence, or over the full bytes if you want signature-binding — but pick one, document it, and never change it. For ed25519, pin your verification semantics (strict / ZIP-215) and state it in the spec, because permissive and strict verifiers disagreeing on a signature is a chain split.",
          "9. UNBOUNDED ANYTHING. Symptom: a single peer OOMs your entire validator set. Causes: a mempool with no global byte cap and no per-sender cap (one address submits 10M txs with nonce gaps and every node holds them all in Queued forever); gossipsub with no `max_transmit_size`; a sync request handler that honours 'give me blocks 0 to 100,000,000' in one response; a decoder with recursive types and no depth limit (a 40-byte input inflates to a stack overflow); a `Vec::with_capacity(n)` where `n` is a length prefix read from the network. Fix, at every network boundary: a byte cap, a count cap, a recursion-depth cap, and a per-peer rate limit — and `with_capacity(min(n, LIMIT))` never `with_capacity(n)`. Mempool specifically: global cap (32 MiB), per-sender cap (64 txs), and evict lowest-fee-first with a TTL.",
          "10. ONE GLOBAL LOCK OVER NODE STATE. Symptom: RPC p99 latency of several seconds under load; or a hard deadlock where the node stops producing blocks and no thread is running. Causes, by language: Rust — holding a `Mutex`/`RwLock` guard across an `.await`, or calling a synchronous redb/rocksdb read from inside an async task and starving the tokio worker pool; Go — a `sync.RWMutex` on a shared state struct that every goroutine takes, plus goroutine leaks when a channel is never drained on shutdown; Node — doing signature verification on the main event loop so a 1,000-tx block's verification stalls consensus for 60ms+. Fix: single-writer actor with bounded channels and `oneshot` replies (Malachite's `Reply<T> = oneshot::Sender<T>` shape); readers take `Arc<Snapshot>` at a version and never block the writer; all synchronous DB work goes through `spawn_blocking` or a dedicated thread pool; deny `clippy::await_holding_lock` in CI; thread `context.Context` through every Go channel operation; move crypto to `worker_threads` in Node.",
          "11. NO CONSENSUS WAL — SIGNING BEFORE FSYNC. Symptom: a validator crashes, restarts, and votes differently for the same (height, round, step) than it did before the crash, producing equivocation evidence against itself and getting slashed for a bug that was not malicious. Fix: the anti-double-sign high-water mark `(height, round, step)` must be fsync'd *before* the signature leaves the signer, and it must live inside the `Signer` implementation — not in the consensus state — so it survives a consensus bug, a DB rollback, and an operator accidentally running two nodes with one key. Malachite ships a `wal` crate for exactly this; CometBFT has had one since 2016.",
          "12. NO REORG / EVICTION PATH IN THE MEMPOOL. Symptom (even on an instant-finality chain): transactions that were in a block that got replaced, or that were reaped but whose block was never committed, silently disappear and users' transactions 'vanish'. Fix: `on_new_head` must (a) remove committed hashes, (b) re-add transactions from any block that was reaped-but-not-committed, (c) recheck the remaining Pending set against the new state version, and (d) promote Queued entries whose nonce gap just closed. Reth's four-sub-pool model exists for exactly this bookkeeping. On a Tendermint-style chain you get to skip fork choice entirely, but you do NOT get to skip this.",
          "13. UNCHECKED ARITHMETIC IN THE STATE TRANSITION. Symptom: a balance underflows to 2^128-1 and one account owns the entire supply; or total supply drifts and nobody notices for 40,000 blocks. Cause: `balance - amount` instead of `checked_sub`, and reward/fee math that adds before it checks. In Rust, release builds wrap silently while debug builds panic — so this class of bug is invisible in your tests and live in production. Fix: `#![deny(clippy::arithmetic_side_effects)]` in the executor crate, forcing `checked_*`/`saturating_*` everywhere; and a total-supply invariant asserted at the end of every `execute()` in debug builds and behind a feature flag in release.",
          "14. PANICKING ON BAD INPUT INSIDE THE STATE TRANSITION. Symptom: one malformed transaction included by any proposer halts every node in the network simultaneously — the worst possible outcome, because it is remotely triggerable by anyone who can get bytes into a block. Cause: `unwrap()`, `expect()`, array indexing, `panic!` on a validation failure, or a Go `nil` map write anywhere in the tx-handling path. Fix: `deny(clippy::unwrap_used, clippy::indexing_slicing)` in the executor crate; every tx handler returns `Result<TxResult, TxError>` and a `TxError` is a *deterministic failed transaction*, never a process exit; and a fuzz target that feeds arbitrary bytes as a transaction body to `execute()` and asserts it never panics."
        ],
        "corrections": [
          "ENGINE API IS STALE IN THE SURVEY. The survey cites engine_newPayloadV4 / engine_forkchoiceUpdatedV3 as current. Those are the Prague-fork methods. Amsterdam defines engine_newPayloadV5 (ExecutionPayloadV4 with a blockAccessList field), engine_getPayloadV6, engine_forkchoiceUpdatedV4 (adds a custodyColumns parameter), engine_getBlobsV4, and engine_getPayloadBodiesBy{Hash,Range}V2. The Prague parameter list the survey quoted for newPayloadV4 is otherwise exactly right.",
          "revm IS 43.0.0, NOT 42.0.1. crates.io shows revm 43.0.0 published 2026-08-26. However reth main's Cargo.toml still pins revm = \"42.0.1\" — so 42.0.1 is the right choice if you want reth parity, and that nuance is worth stating rather than just bumping the number.",
          "THE ABCI SPEC DOES NOT ENUMERATE BANNED CONSTRUCTS IN app_requirements.md. That file states the requirements abstractly (Requirements 4, 9, 11, 12). The actual enumerated list lives in spec/abci/abci++_basic_concepts.md under 'Determinism' and has four categories, verbatim: hardware failures (cosmic rays, overheating); node-dependent state (random numbers, time); underspecification (library versions, race conditions, floating point numbers, serialization issues, hash-table iteration); external sources (filesystem, network calls).           "COMETBFT VERSION RESOLUTION TRAP, UNFLAGGED. The survey correctly names CometBFT v0.40.           "COMETBFT DOES NOT DIRECTLY DEPEND ON PEBBLE. The survey says CometBFT and Cosmos SDK 'both now depend on' pebble at v1.1.1 / v1.1.5 in their go.mod files.           "RETH USES resolver = \"2\", NOT 3.           "RETH'S DOCUMENTED SUB-POOLS ARE THREE, NOT FOUR.           "MALACHITE'S CRATES.IO RELEASES ARE A YEAR STALE, AND THE SURVEY'S EFFECT/AppMsg NAMES ARE WRONG. informalsystems-malachitebft-core-consensus and -app-channel are both at 0.5.0, published 2025-08-01.         "value": "The object-centric alternative to global storage: every object has a 32-byte UID, an owner, a version, and the digest of the last transaction that touched it; five ownership types (address-owned, immutable, consensus-address owned/party, shared, wrapped); objects referenced by ID, (ID, version), or the (ID, version, digest) triple. This ownership tagging is what lets owned-object transactions take a consensus fast path."

        "url": "https://docs.arbitrum.io/stylus/gentle-introduction",
        "value": "The most honest published account of the dual-VM cost/benefit: a second coequal WASM VM beside the EVM, a separate metering unit ('ink', thousands of times smaller than gas), a mandatory activation step that compiles to native code and runs safety/metering/memory checks and expires annually, storage costing the same as the EVM (so the win is compute-only), and full Solidity<->WASM interop."

        "value": "Documents the direction of travel away from Wasm for contracts: ink! v6 migrates from pallet-contracts+Wasm (wasmi) to pallet-revive+RISC-V (PolkaVM), with Solidity supported via the revive Yul->LLVM->RISC-V compiler.         "url": "https://docs.monad.xyz/developer-essentials/eip-7702",
        "value": "A concrete case study in how a parallel EVM chain must bend Ethereum semantics: a 10 MON balance floor for delegated EOAs (because Monad reserves a per-EOA budget for consensus-time balance checks on in-flight transactions) and a prohibition on CREATE/CREATE2 inside a delegated-EOA frame (to keep nonce evolution statically predictable). Exactly the class of deviation you will face if you combine 7702 with parallel execution."

        "url": "https://blog.base.dev/postmortem-june-25th-block-production-outage",
        "value": "A 2026 worked example of the invalid-block failure class and its recovery. Root cause: the block builder failed to clear journal state after a transaction failed validation, so a later valid transaction executed against dirty state and produced an incorrect receipts root; validators re-executing with a clean journal rejected the block and the chain halted at 47,806,542. A second bug — a race in engine reset — blocked sequencer resync after restart. Timeline shows alert at +2min, war room at +5min, bad block identified at +6min, root cause at +68min, production resumed at ~116min, and a near-identical second outage the next day. Action items: harden protocol fuzz testing and adversarial transaction patterns, build load-testing harnesses, add graceful recovery to speed ecosystem restart."
